articles.title: Sara Duterte says resignation 'out of the question' amid impeachment trial
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday reiterated that she would not be stepping down from office amid her impeachment trial.

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 5:01pm
Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday reiterated that she would not be stepping down from office amid her impeachment trial.
“No, sir. Resignation, that is out of the question. I already answered that several times during the course of the trial,” Duterte said in a press conference.

“It is something that I cannot do because I feel that it's a betrayal of the 32.2 million people who voted for me, and of course the general public, if I resign from the position of Vice President,” she added.

Vice President Sara Duterte reiterates she would not be stepping down from office amid her impeachment trial: “That’s out of the question…that’s something I cannot do because it’s betrayal to the public.” @gmanews https://t.co/0cqfTRpPmp Other Stories — Giselle Ombay (@giselleombay_) November 27, 2026
The Vice President is currently facing an impeachment trial before the Senate impeachment court.

Her defense team has been presenting evidence and witnesses for Article II of the impeachment case, alleging her unexplained wealth due to her supposed failure to truthfully disclose assets in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), and failure to divest in businesses as constitutionally required for the President and Vice President.
Preparing for worst
Duterte also admitted that she and her defense team are always “preparing for the worst” now that the trial is nearing its end and the Senate impeachment court is expected to issue a verdict soon.

“Because if there's an acquittal, it will just be a continuation of what we are doing now for the Office of the Vice President. So next year, all the projects and all the programs will be implemented as if it's 2026 or 2025 or 2024—a matter of difference of budget,” she explained.
“But if it's a verdict of guilty, it will come with a lot of consequences,” she added.
The Vice President said her primary concern, if she is ever convicted in her impeachment trial, is the expected loss of employment in the OVP.
She said around 300 families of employees from various OVP satellite offices across the country may be affected by the possible conviction.
“Because the satellite offices are coterminous to me as Vice President. So that is our first worry, the jobs of those OVP employees who are coterminous,” she said.
Duterte also said she is preparing to ask those stationed in the OVP headquarters in Mandaluyong City to move out if she gets convicted.
“So those are the things that we need to prepare for. But if it's a verdict of acquittal, then we don't have to prepare for anything except for the rollout of projects for 2027,” she said.
Acceptance
Nevertheless, Duterte said she will accept whatever the decision will be at the end of the trial—whether she will get acquitted or convicted.

“We will accept whatever it is that the judgment of the Senate impeachment court will give for the impeachment trial, and we will all have to live with the consequences of this out-of-mind decision of President Marcos,” she said.
Malacañang has repeatedly said that President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. is not influencing the impeachment proceedings against the Vice President.—AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Supreme Court to render its decision on Quebec's secularism law today
articles.summary: On Friday morning, a record number of journalists and lawyers of record who've been sworn to confidentiality will be the first to read a historic judgment from the Supreme Court of Canada determining…

image.caption: The grand hall of the temporary Supreme Court of Canada, located in the West Memorial Building in Ottawa is hosting, by far, the largest lockup in its history as journalists and legal teams await the top court's ruling on Bill 21. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

On Friday morning, a record number of journalists and lawyers of record who've been sworn to confidentiality will be the first to read a historic judgment from the Supreme Court of Canada determining the fate of Quebec's controversial Bill 21.
Judgment addressing the challenge to Bill 21 will be released at 9:45 a.m. ET

On Friday morning, journalists and lawyers of record who've been sworn to confidentiality will be the first to read a historic judgment from the Supreme Court of Canada determining the fate of Quebec's controversial Bill 21.
The 90-minute lockup will be the biggest in the top court's history, hosting legal teams for 51 individuals, groups and governments from across the country, including six auditors general.
All those eyes will pore over a judgment that could overturn Bill 21, Quebec's secularism law preventing some public-sector workers from wearing religious symbols while on the job.
The court could also rein in the use of the notwithstanding clause, which allows provinces and the federal government to override some Charter rights for five-year renewable increments.
It could also do neither of these things — simply uphold the law in its current form and leave issues around the notwithstanding clause alone.
No matter what the outcome, however, the judgment will be historic.

items: What's at stake as Canada's top court ruling on Quebec secularism law looms
6 key moments from the Supreme Court challenge of Quebec's secularism law

blocks.text: Bill 21, the Act respecting the laicity of the State, became law on June 19, 2019.
It prohibits the wearing of religious symbols including but not limited to hijabs, turbans, yarmulkes, crucifixes and Sikh kirpans by some public service workers while they're on the job.

When the law was first passed, it specifically impacted educators like teachers and principals, police officers, government lawyers and even members of the province's legislature, including Quebec's minister of justice and the Speaker of the National Assembly.
Groups challenging Quebec secularism law in Supreme Court say it breaches basic rights
The law also required these public-sector workers to do their jobs with their faces uncovered unless they need it covered for non-religious reasons such as a health issue or disability.
For security or identity verification reasons, people can be denied access to public services unless they also have their faces uncovered.
Bill 21 has resulted in job losses across the province as people change professions or move to other parts of the country to escape the law.
Overriding Charter protections

All of those provisions violated civil liberty protections in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and Quebec's Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, but Bill 21 became law anyway because both charters have an override clause.

The notwithstanding clause, Section 33 of the federal Charter, can override certain sections — including Section 2 and sections 7 to 15, which deal with fundamental freedoms, legal rights and equality rights.
Once invoked, Section 33 prevents any judicial review of the legislation in question. After five years, the clause ceases to have any effect — unless it is re-enacted.

Bill 21 also invoked the Quebec Charter's version of the notwithstanding clause, Section 52, which allows rights from Section 1 to Section 38 to be overridden until the National Assembly in Quebec repeals the law.
Challenging Bill 21

In April of 2021 the Quebec Superior Court ruled on a constitutional challenge to Bill 21, largely upholding the law while at the same time finding some constitutional rights had been improperly overridden.

The court said Bill 21 improperly violated Section 3 of the federal Charter by interfering with protected democratic rights because it would prevent people from serving in elected office. The law remained in effect but could not apply to members of the Quebec legislature.

The court also ruled that Bill 21 violated minority language education rights guaranteed by Section 23 of the federal Charter — which includes the management and control over minority language institutions.

In early 2024 the Quebec Court of Appeal mostly upheld the lower court's decision but it tossed out the section on minority language rights, saying it did not impact the content of what was taught, only who was hired to teach it.
Top court has its say
Seven justices of the Supreme Court of Canada heard the case over four days in March, which the court says was one of the longest-ever hearings for a case at Canada's top court.
Over those four days it was asked to weigh in on a number of questions including:

items: Whether Bill 21 is constitutionally valid.
Whether the notwithstanding clause was properly used.
Whether there are limits on use of the clause.
Whether a court can issue a non-binding declaration saying that while the law stands — because of the notwithstanding clause — it still violates certain rights.
Whether the federal Charter's guarantee of equal rights for both males and females in Section 28 has been violated by Bill 21.
Whether Bill 21 infringes on English-language education rights under Section 23 of the federal Charter.
Whether the face-uncovering requirement for National Assembly members violated democratic rights in Section 3 of the Charter.
Whether Bill 21 is consistent with certain pre-Confederation laws.

blocks.text: The Supreme Court can pick and choose which of these questions it decides need settling. It can also refer one or more questions back to lower courts with guidance on how to proceed.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Peter Zimonjic is a senior writer for CBC News who reports for digital, radio and television. He has worked as a reporter and columnist in London, England, for the Telegraph, Times and Daily Mail, and in Canada for the Ottawa Citizen, Torstar and Sun Media. He is the author of Into The Darkness: An Account of 7/7, published by Vintage.

articles.title: This Independent is giving Poilievre's Conservatives the jitters ahead of a crucial byelection
articles.summary: The federal riding of Brantford-Brant South has been a Conservative stronghold for most of the last 20 years. But an insurgent Independent candidate who was passed over by leader Pierre Poilievre is…

image.caption: Independent candidate Dave Carrol is running in the upcoming federal byelection in Brantford-Brant South. A local pastor, Carrol was running for the Conservative nomination but was snubbed by the party brass. (Raphael Tremblay/CBC)

blocks.text: The federal riding of Brantford-Brant South has been a Conservative stronghold for most of the last 20 years. But an insurgent Independent candidate who was passed over by leader Pierre Poilievre is trying to stop Tory rule in an upcoming byelection — and there are early signs he's gaining traction.
That candidate is Dave Carrol, a pastor at Freedom House — a big church with a long list of parishioners — and a local media personality with regular segments on Rogers TV.

Those positions, plus his decades of advocacy on issues like homelessness, and his "Captain Kindness" superhero persona at community events like the Santa Claus parade, have made him a known quantity in this mid-sized industrial city in Ontario's southwest.
With endorsements from past Conservative MPs in the area, including Phil McColeman and the outgoing Larry Brock, Carrol sought the party's nomination for the Dec. 7 vote.

items: Highest MP turnover rate in decades making for byelection bonanza this Parliament

blocks.text: But he never had the chance to test his support among the party faithful. Poilievre unilaterally appointed ex-mayor Kevin Davis as the candidate, upsetting Carrol and his supporters who thought he was best placed to keep the seat for the blue team. The party has since revoked his membership.
After being snubbed, Carrol struck out on his own, cobbling together the campaign team and resources needed to take on the Liberal-Conservative duopoly in this area.
If the election sign war is any indication, Carrol is poised to do better than most independents who vie for a seat in the House of Commons.
Parts of the city are blanketed with Carrol signs emblazoned with his campaign slogan: "People first. Community always."
In some neighbourhoods, the Carrol signs easily outnumber the Conservative ones.

If the election sign war is any indication, Dave Carrol is poised to do better than most independents who vie for a seat in the House of Commons. Parts of Brantford are blanketed with Carrol signs. (Raphael Tremblay/CBC)
In an interview with CBC News, one of his first with a national news organization since his Conservative candidacy went awry, Carrol said this campaign is not about getting even with Poilievre.

"I've spent most of my adult life dressed up in a Captain Kindness costume, walking around talking about how to use kindness to transform a community. What I'm doing has absolutely nothing to do with revenge," he said.
But he said the party's move to block his candidacy and usurp the will of some local Conservative members did inspire him to jump into the fray.
'Not a revenge vote'
"We are frustrated with this decline in democracy," Carrol said.
"But this has not been a personal endeavour. This is not a revenge vote. This is not a protest vote. This is a purposeful choice to put people's voices at the forefront."
And so far, he said, the reception has been "tremendous," as his message of tackling the scourge of homelessness and addiction has resonated in a part of the province hit hard by both.
Still, he's cognizant of what a victory could mean for Poilievre and the Conservatives.
"There's a national spotlight because this is a consequential election," he said. "The people I talk to are not nervous, they're excited."
Brantford campaign has 'absolutely nothing to do with revenge,' Independent candidate says
But some federal Conservatives are feeling skittish.

This particular byelection has the potential to be hugely consequential for Poilievre given it's the one riding out of the six up for grabs that is most likely to change hands next month, according to a recent survey by Abacus Data. Brock won the seat by about 11 percentage points in the last federal election but Conservative support nationally has fallen off since then.
Poilievre has been a frequent presence in the riding this fall, often giving up his weekends to door-knock in a seat that could decide his fate.

There have been six federal byelections so far this year and the Conservatives have lost them all. Party sources told CBC News that if the Conservatives fall short in Brantford, it could ignite a movement to oust Poilievre as leader as some MPs grow restless after a prolonged losing streak.

One Conservative source described Brantford as Poilievre's "Toronto-St. Paul's moment," a reference to the 2024 Liberal byelection loss in a party stronghold that was the beginning of the end for former prime minister Justin Trudeau.
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is seen on Parliament Hill on Thursday. Poilievre has been been in Brantford often in the lead up to the December byelection. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)
Speaking to reporters on Parliament Hill this week, Conservative MP Ben Lobb said this election could be a nail-biter.
"I don't think anybody knows how that is actually going to go," Lobb said. "I think everybody would say it's close. So really, on that one, it's whoever gets out the vote."
Poilievre, meanwhile, has bristled at questions about what this Brantford byelection could mean for his tenure at the top.
"You all ask this question again and again and again over the last several days," Poilievre said at a news conference this week.

"I think we actually have to focus in the byelections on the simple questions: Can you afford your groceries more today than when Mark Carney became prime minister? Or is it time to lower costs with a Conservative approach?" he said.

items: Defence minister 'very concerned' after Poilievre claims constituent's job was threatened

blocks.text: While Liberal candidate Joy O'Donnell, a local businessperson, is a serious contender for the seat given the party's recent strength in national polls, the Conservatives have so far focused their negative campaign messaging on Carrol.
In some homes across Brantford, voters have received direct mail from the Conservatives with a warning of what they say could happen: "A vote for Dave Carrol is a vote for the Liberals."
Carrol said he's not splitting the Conservative vote, claiming he's drawing support from voters of all political stripes who are tired of a party-dominated, "Ottawa knows best" approach.
"We have people who have not just voted for, but served across the political spectrum," he said.

Carrol is seen in his 'campaign cottage' in Brantford. Without access to sophisticated party databases, his campaign is relying on a team of dedicated volunteers to help him do what's not often done in Canadian politics: win as an Independent. (Raphael Tremblay/CBC)
Carrol's Conservative opponent, was not available for an interview.
"As he approaches the final stretch of the campaign, Kevin is prioritizing his time at the doors, connecting directly with voters," a party spokesperson said of Davis.
Carrol doesn't have access to the sophisticated voter databases used by the big parties to track supporters and turn them out.

items: How to vote in the upcoming federal byelection for Brantford—Brant South

blocks.text: But there's a steady stream of campaign volunteers through Carrol's quaint office that he's taken to calling his "campaign cottage," given its rustic nature compared to the relatively more comfortable digs of Davis's strip mall election outpost just a few blocks away.
The campaign is doing things the old-fashioned way, sending its committed roster of volunteers out with a map and a clipboard to collect the names and phone numbers of potential Carrol supporters.
Independent Brantford byelection candidate disputes vote splitting after Conservative snubbing

While it's always an uphill battle as an Independent, Carrol said voters in this part of the Ontario heartland have a recent history of eschewing party politics and backing an independent candidate with deep roots in the community.

Ontario MPP Bobbi Ann Brady from the neighbouring Haldimand-Norfolk riding has a similar story. A longtime community advocate, she was passed over for the PC nomination when the party appointed a candidate and then ran as an Independent. Brady has since won the seat twice, with huge margins.
"I am fired up because I genuinely care about this. For me, this is not about politics. It's about people," Carrol said.
"And so do I think we have a chance of winning this? I absolutely do."

articles.title: The corruption case against Benjamin Netanyahu just suffered a serious blow. What comes next?
articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was handed a major legal victory this week when the judges in the years-long corruption trial against him suggested the prosecution reconsider one case, work…

image.caption: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to the media after voting at a polling station in Jerusalem in October. (Jewel Samad/AFPThe Associated Press)

blocks.text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was handed a major legal victory this week when the judges in the years-long corruption trial against him suggested the prosecution reconsider one case, work out a plea deal in another and entirely drop the third — the most serious.

While the court clarified these were recommendations and not rulings, it was still a significant blow to the prosecution, which has sought to convict the prime minister on a series of charges related to allegations of bribery, fraud and breach of trust after he was indicted in 2019.
The prime minister has denied any wrongdoing, casting the charges as a witch hunt by hostile media, police and prosecutors.
But now, the future of the trial is in serious doubt as prosecutors decide how to proceed.
Here's a look at the cases, the charges, what the judges said and where it may go next.
Israeli judges call to drop 1 of Netanyahu's 3 corruption charges
What is Netanyahu charged with?
Netanyahu is facing charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate cases known as case 1000, case 2000 and case 4000.
On Wednesday, the judges overseeing the trial summoned Israel's Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara to appear at the Jerusalem District Court.

"That never happens," Yael Friedman, the legal correspondent for the Israeli newspaper Haaretz, told CBC News. She has been covering the trial since it began in May 2020. "You just need to understand that it was a very irregular act."
Speaking for the court, Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman proceeded to lay out their concerns or recommendations for each of the three cases.
Case 1000
Charges: fraud, breach of trust
In this case, Netanyahu is accused of accepting nearly $200,000 in gifts from Hollywood producer Arnon Milchan and Australian billionaire James Packer.

Film producer Arnon Milchan leaves the Old Ship Hotel in Brighton, England, on on June 25, 2023, after giving testimony in Benjamin Netanyahu's corruption trial. His testimony was transmitted via videolink to the District Court of Jerusalem. Prosecutors allege Milchan gave the Israeli prime minister expensive gifts in return for personal favours. (Chris Eades/Getty Images)
Prosecutors allege that Netanyahu lobbied on Milchan’s behalf on U.S. visa matters, tried to legislate a generous tax break for him and sought to promote his interests in the Israeli media market.
What the judges said: Work out a plea deal or settlement

“It seems to us that it is possible to get to a conclusion," Friedman-Feldman said, according to the Times of Israel. "We are open to all possibilities — we need to find the procedural way to get there."

Friedman told CBC News that she believes the court was suggesting that though there could be a conviction, the two sides should instead get together to come up with some kind of plea arrangement to finish the trial.
Case 2000
This case centres around two audio recordings of conversations between Netanyahu and Arnon Mozes in 2014.
Mozes is the the publisher of Yedioth Ahronoth, one of Israel's largest newspapers and Ynet, one of the largest news websites.

Arnon Mozes, left, the owner and publisher of Yedioth Ahronoth, one of Israel's leading newspapers, is seen in Lod, Israel, in January 2017. At right, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and U.S. President Donald Trump speak at the White House in January 2020, as U.S. casino magnate Sheldon Adelson looks on. (Reuters, Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Netanyahu was accused of offering to put forward legislation that would have helped restrict the circulation of the free daily newspaper Israel Hayom, also known as Israel Today, which is the main rival to Mozes' paper.
The irony is that Israel Hayom (Israel Today) is owned by the family of Sheldon Adelson, the late U.S. billionaire and casino magnate, who was also a supporter of Netanyahu.
Mozes has denied any wrongdoing.
What the judges said: Reconsider
The judges recommended prosecutors reconsider case 2000.
"Legally, this is a very, very problematic, case," said Moshe Cohen-Eliya, law professor and former president of the Tel Aviv-based College of Law and Business.

"What the court actually said is that basically there is no legal offence," Cohen-Eliya said in an interview with CBC News. "Maybe you have very good evidence about these kinds of negotiation between Netanyahu and Mozes. However there is no offence."
According to Friedman, the judge said that while she doesn't see the court convicting Netanyahu on case 2000, she gave the prosecution a chance to explain the charges.
"They're leaving it a bit open," Friedman said.
Case 4000
Charges: bribery, fraud, breach of trust
This was considered the most serious of the three cases as it includes the charge of bribery.

Netanyahu, while serving as both primer minister and communications minister from 2014 to 2017, was accused of seeking to ease regulations that would have benefitted Shaul Elovitch, then the controlling shareholder in Bezeq, Israel's largest telecommunications company.

Israeli businessman Shaul Elovitch appears in the Justice Court in Tel Aviv in one of the graft probes threatening Netanyahu on Feb. 22, 2018. Elovitch is accused of having given Netanyahu positive coverage on his Walla news site in exchange for policies benefiting his telecommunications business. (Jack Guez/AFP/Getty Images)
In return, it's alleged that the news website Walla, owned by Elovitch at the time, would provide positive coverage of Netanyahu and his family.
The regulatory favours would be worth around ⁠1.8 billion shekels (about $500 million US) to Bezeq.
Elovitch has denied any wrongdoing.
What the judges said: Consider dropping the charges

As for case 4000, in relation to the bribery charge, Friedman-Feldman said there was "serious doubt as to whether the evidentiary basis supports this claim." The Times of Israel reported that she said "the chances of conviction are low" for all three charges.

This wasn't the first time the judges have raised concerns about the ability to prove the bribery charge. In May 2023, judges said prosecutors should consider withdrawing the charge, but the prosecutors declined to do so.

"So, from that perspective, it was already kind of like known that [the bribery charge] was the more weaker charge," Friedman said. "But what was surprising was how they basically overruled the whole 4000 case."
Has Netanyahu testified?
Netanyahu has testified in 98 hearings in 18 months of the trial, while Israel was at war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

"It was quite crazy, the situation where he gets, like, this note from one of his secretaries saying he needs to take an urgent call," Friedman said. "And he goes up to the judges and says, 'Um, excuse me, I need to take a break.' "

She says Netanyahu's testimony, which included many breaks within the 18 month time span, is the longest in Israel's history of criminal trials, and also notes that Netanyahu would show up for the testimony of major witnesses.
On Wednesday, the judges overseeing the trial summoned Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara to appear at the Jerusalem District Court. (Gil Cohen-Magen/The Associated Press)
What will the prosecution do?
The prosecution said it will take time to review the recommendations of the court. But Cohen-Eliya said he believes the attorney general will ignore the judges and continue with the trial.
"I can guess that she would go back to the court, and she would say, 'I heard you, but I'm still pursuing the case,' " he said.
Cohen-Eliya says the corruption case against Netanyahu is the most important one in Israel's history besides the trial of Nazi Adolf Eichmann in the 1960s.
"It's a lot at stake for the prosecution," he said.

Friedman says if the prosecutors "believe in the case and think that the judges are wrong" they could continue with the trial, get a verdict — even one that goes against them — and then appeal to the Israeli Supreme Court.
Another option, she says, is to start negotiating a plea deal.
"And then it depends how much they would want to compromise. And what would Netanyahu agree [to] compromise from his side?"

articles.title: Small businesses worry potential consumer pullback could cut into critical holiday sales
articles.summary: The holiday shopping season is a critical money-making time for lots of retailers. But as retail sales point to a dip in consumer spending, small business owners worry a pullback by shoppers could…

image.caption: As the busy holiday shopping season gets underway, small business owners are worried consumers might cut back on spending this year, denting their sales. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

blocks.text: Business

The holiday shopping season is a critical money-making time for lots of retailers. But as retail sales point to a dip in consumer spending, small business owners worry a pullback by shoppers could dent their sales.
Pullback in spending biggest threat to holiday sales, according to survey of independent business owners
It's the most wonderful — and most important — time of the year for retailers like Kristi Wozniak: the holiday shopping season.
"It's very big," said Wozniak, owner and founder of Keylime Activewear in Sherwood Park, Alta. "We are in our busiest season right now for sure."
Wozniak says a quarter of her sales come from holiday shopping, with December being their busiest month.
But sales have been down recently compared to previous years, and she's worried that shoppers slowing their spending could cut into those critical holiday sales.
"Customers are definitely more cautious where they're spending their dollars," Wozniak said.
She's not alone. As small businesses struggle with tariffs and rising costs, some are worried that less spending by consumers this holiday season could deal another blow.
Kristi Wozniak, owner of Keylime Athletics, stands beside a sign advertising discounts at her storefront in Sherwood Park, Alta. (Submitted by Kristi Wozniak)

In a survey of 1,675 of its members from across the country, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business found that the holiday season is an important part of the financial outlook for four in 10 respondents. And 73 per cent of that group said a pullback in spending posed the biggest threat to holiday sales.

"In times of worsening affordability in the middle of a trade war, lack of consumer demand has actually been a key threat for many small businesses," said Ryan Mitton, the CFIB's director of legislative affairs for B.C.
And retail sales data from Statistics Canada shows consumers might, in fact, be trying to cut down on their spending.

Retail sales ticked up in September by 0.8 per cent — but that was driven mostly by a jump in how much consumers were spending at gas stations. And an early estimate for October forecasted a 1.5 per cent drop in retail sales.

items: Food and shelter have driven Canada's affordability crisis. Health care isn't far behind

blocks.text: Those figures give a "very weak kickoff point" for retail sales in the last quarter of the year, according to Michael Davenport, a senior economist with Oxford Economics.

He says high gas prices due to the war in Iran have been squeezing household budgets, while the weak job market and volatility in financial markets are weighing on consumer's confidence. And while consumer spending has been pretty resilient throughout the year despite some of those factors, he expects they'll cause Canadians to spend less in coming months.

items: Canadian economy lost 4,700 jobs in October as unemployment rate ticked up to 6.7%

blocks.text: "All of these factors are kind of coming together, we think, to lead to a bit of a slowdown in consumer spending growth towards the end of 2026 and early 2027."
Black Friday deal hunting with AI? What chatbots can miss
If holiday sales do take a hit, Wozniak says it could leave her with less cash to order new stock in the new year and force her to cut back some hours for staff.
"[If] we didn't make enough money for the previous season, now we're looking for cashflow options," Wozniak said.
She's stopped purchasing from some of her U.S. suppliers due to tariffs and to keep down costs related to shipping and the unfavorable exchange rate between the Canadian and U.S. dollar.
But rising manufacturing costs have still shrunken her profit margins in recent years, meaning she can't offer massive Black Friday discounts on clothing at Keylime like big box stores can.

items: Can AI chatbots really help shoppers find the best deals?
You told us how you're keeping holiday costs down this year

blocks.text: Despite that, she's offering deals on gift cards and discounts that scale with the number of items shoppers buy, which she hopes will be enough to get buyers through the door — and spending some of their cash.
"We do want to attract the customer into the store," Wozniak said. "We try our hardest."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.

blocks.text: Welcome to DW's coverage of what Germany is talking about on Friday, 27 November. Catch up on yesterday's news here.
November 27, 2026
German parliament to vote on €556 billion budget for 2027
German lawmakers will on Friday vote on a federal budget for 2027 which foresees €556 billion ($610 billion) in government spending, around €31 billion more than in 2026.
The largest chunk of expenditure (just over €200 billion) will go on federal contributions to the statutory pension system, while €110 billion is to be allocated to defense – a 32.7% increase.

The plans call for around €210 billion in fresh borrowing, a figure which is only expected to increase between now and 2030, while €2.7 billion are also expected to be shifted away from Germany's climate protection and transformation fund.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and their Social Democrat (SPD) coalition partners have spent an unusually long time wrangling over the budget, with Merz finally clinching a deal last week after more than eight hours of talks at the Chancellery.

articles.title: Guinea-Bissau's military leaders delay return to civilian rule until 2028
articles.summary: The announcement comes a year after a military coup with its leaders promising a return to civilian rule within 12 months.

blocks.text: Guinea-Bissau's military rulers have postponed elections scheduled for next week by two years, delaying the return to civilian rule.
Transitional President Gen Horta N'Tam announced in a decree that the presidential and parliamentary elections, originally due on 6 December, would now take place on 26 November 2028.
The announcement came exactly a year after the military seized power, promising to return the country to civilian rule within 12 months.
In a statement, the presidency said an assessment of electoral preparations had found that there were insufficient "technical, material and financial conditions" to hold the polls as planned.
It said the delay would provide more time to ensure the elections were credible, transparent and inclusive, with all candidates given equal opportunities.
The presidency also reiterated its commitment to holding the country's first-ever local government elections but gave no date for the vote.
Gen N'Tam was sworn in as transitional president a day after the military overthrew President Umaro Sissoco Embaló in November 2025.
The coup took place three days after general elections and a day before provisional results were due to be announced.
Both Embaló and his main challenger, Fernando Dias, had claimed victory.
Embaló, who has since been living in exile in Morocco, was barred from returning to Guinea-Bissau last month, despite expressing an interest in contesting the elections.
Guinea-Bissau has experienced several coups and attempted coups since gaining independence from Portugal in 1974.

articles.title: VP Sara Duterte: We will accept whatever impeachment verdict
articles.summary: The Office of the Vice President is ready to accept whatever verdict the Senate impeachment court issues, Vice President Sara Duterte said in a press conference.

blocks.text: November 27, 2026 | 4:53pm

Vice President Sara Duterte chats with Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and Senate President Pro Tempore Tito Sotto as she attends the Senate deliberations on the Office of the Vice President’s budget for 2027 on November 26, 2026.
The STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Vice President is ready to accept whatever verdict the Senate impeachment court issues, Vice President Sara Duterte said in a press conference on Friday, November 27.
Duterte told reporters that her office is “prepared for the worst,” saying that the OVP has discussed how to address the consequences that could come with a guilty verdict.
She said that the office’s primary concern is the loss of employment among staff whose tenure depends on Duterte’s position.
The OVP estimates that Duterte’s removal from office would result in the termination of these employees, affecting around 300 families nationwide.

The office has also discussed relocating to a different physical space, as its current address in Mandaluyong City was selected because it served as Duterte’s campaign headquarters during the 2022 elections.
Duterte also cited the possibility of public backlash over her removal, saying that voters could take issue with replacing an elected official with an appointee.
If Duterte is impeached, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. would have to nominate someone from Congress to fill her position.
Malacañang earlier said that Marcos has not decided on the vice president’s replacement.

An acquittal, meanwhile, would have little impact on the office’s operations, Duterte said, as it would allow the OVP to continue its current activities and focus on implementing its planned projects.
Duterte added that even in the event of an acquittal, her opposition would still have a year to launch another impeachment attempt or “do many other things” to her.

“By that time (a third impeachment case) siguro, mag-resign na ako kasi wala na talaga akong pambayad ng abogado … Puwede nila akong ipakulong. Puwede nila akong ipadala sa Pluto or sa ilalim ng lupa. Depende sa kanila.”

(By that time [a third impeachment case], I’ll probably resign because I don’t have money to pay for a lawyer anymore. They can have me imprisoned. They can have me sent to Pluto or buried underground. It depends on what they want.)
Asked if she would appear at the impeachment court to receive her verdict in person, Duterte said that she was still unsure, citing activities scheduled in Davao in December.
The vice president’s camp and members of the prosecution have both floated the possibility of the trial ending before the end of the year.
The Senate impeachment court has set hearings from December 1 to 4, with the vice president’s dentist and a Bureau of Customs official expected to take the witness stand.
The witnesses’ testimonies form part of Duterte’s defense against the second article of impeachment, which concerns her alleged unexplained wealth.

articles.title: X launches parental controls to help manage teen use
articles.summary: The parental controls feature launch comes some 20 years after X, formerly Twitter, was built

blocks.text: The parental controls feature launch comes some 20 years after X, formerly Twitter, was built

items: Social media platform X has introduced parental controls to help parents guide their teens' usage of the platform.
The controls allow parents to monitor usage time, set limits, approve new followers, and filter content, while ensuring teens maintain ownership of their accounts.
This feature marks the addition of parental controls in X's 20-year history, and is likely a response to concerns about the platform's safety for younger users.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Social media platform X on Thursday, November 26, announced it had introduced parental controls so that parents or guardians could better guide teens on their X usage and experiences on it.
The parental controls will not allow parents or guardians to read private messages, see searches or viewing history, post as their teen, or access a given teen account.

The social media platform, in its announcement, acknowledged that “while X is not designed for or promoted to children, and users must be at least 13 or older where required by law, we take extra care with the young people who are here.”

According to the X announcement, teen accounts “default to protected mode, sensitive media is restricted, and targeted advertising is blocked,” while parental controls give families further tools aside from these standard settings for teens.
The new parental control tools will let parents do the following:

items: see how much time their teen has spent on X over the past week
set limits on X usage
require approval for new followers (this also makes the account private)
limit For You recommendations and videos to accounts the teen already follows
control who can send direct messages to the account
filter specific words
turn off sensitive media content
see which accounts a teen has chatted with one-on-one (without seeing what they’ve written)

blocks.text: The X parental controls announcement is a long time coming. The feature addition is a first after about 20 years of operation, and comes after issues with X’s Grok AI chatbot being a vector for the generation of sexualized images or material featuring women and minors.
According to TechCrunch, while X is not generally aimed at teens, a 2024 study pointed to nearly a third of Gen Alpha kids as having an X account.
Michael O’Herlihy, head of safety at X, said in their press announcement that they aim to strike a balance between parental supervision and letting teens have some freedom to be themselves.

“Parents want practical tools, and teens deserve room to grow,” O’Herlihy said. “With Parental Controls on X, families can set the guardrails that fit their home, while teens keep ownership of their accounts and can see every change.”
A more thorough explanation of the parental control settings is available on this Help Center page. – Rappler.com

articles.title: At critical juncture, Friedrich Merz finds Germans’ support for Ukraine wavering
articles.summary:
German chancellor is on difficult terrain, at home and abroad, as he fights to maintain European backing for Kyiv

The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, is navigating choppy waters both at…

blocks.text: The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, is navigating choppy waters both at home and abroad over his insistence that Europe must keep up support – both military and financial – for Ukraine.

At a Brussels summit on Thursday, Merz reiterated his view that all EU member states – pointedly, “not 23 or 24” – should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. He has threatened to veto the bloc’s budget unless all countries sign up to the loan, a stance that saw him accused of “classic blackmail” by Robert Fico, the populist prime minister of Slovakia. Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria have also voiced their misgivings, to varying degrees, over Berlin’s dogged position.

But, unhappily for Merz, he cannot rely on the wholehearted support of the German public, either. A new survey released this week showed that, for the first time, Kyiv no longer enjoys majority support among the German population. The study by the Körber Foundation, showed 53% of those questioned were against Germany supporting Ukraine militarily, with only 46% in favour – compared with 59% just a year ago.

Merz, whose disapproval ratings stand at a record 88%, is therefore looking increasingly isolated. This all sends a worrying signal to Kyiv, which has counted on Germany as its biggest backer for some time, since Washington largely withdrew its favour.

The government’s attempts to push the case for Ukraine domestically now, when it is arguably most necessary, are not helped by the fact that German leaders have been reluctant to play up the support Germany has given to Kyiv since 2022 for fear of stoking embers of resentment.

This extends to keeping as quiet as possible about the estimated 1.33 million Ukrainians who have been given refuge in Germany since the full-scale invasion of their country, because of the strong tendency of the far-right, anti-immigrant Alternative für Deutschland to portray them as a burden.

As the cost of living crisis bites and the German public feels increasingly poorer economically, the debate over Ukraine funding is being framed – misleadingly, say critics – as a contest between the nation’s living standards and the billions paid to Ukraine’s defence.

This week Merz faced down opposition MPs in the Bundestag, the most vociferous from the pro-Kremlin AfD, who called for funding to Ukraine to be halted, as parliament debated the budget for 2027, Germany’s largest ever, due to be voted on by the weekend.

Opposition, however, is not only coming from the right. In Saxony-Anhalt, where in December the AfD may take over a state premiership for the first time, the BSW, a small, Russia-friendly, leftwing party, last month teamed up with the AfD to also demand a halt to arms supplies to Ukraine and the lifting of economic sanctions against Russia.
And on Thursday, an influential former Protestant church leader, pacifist and theologian, Margot Käßmann, called for a “change of course” and more diplomacy from the government.

“We must do everything we can to prevent war,” Käßmann said in an interview with DLF, a public broadcaster, insisting she would not bend to demands for Germans to defend themselves, instead calling for “much more diplomatic commitment”. She also accused Merz of not taking the “discomfort of the population seriously”.

Notably, the Körber survey found that the lowest support for Ukraine, 31%, was recorded in Germany’s eastern states, where the AfD – nationally five points ahead of Merz’s conservative CDU/CSU alliance in the polls – has an increasing hold on power. Only 11% of east Germans are in favour of military help to Ukraine, while 75% would like to see a “normalisation” of relations with Russia, the survey found.
Merz now faces an uphill battle to win the German people round to his own government’s conviction that support for Ukraine is vital if Germany is to ensure its own security and future.

Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano clarified on Friday that his suggestion for contributions of P170,000 each from Filipinos to pay the country’s foreign debt was primarily directed to the richest of the rich, adding that it was only voluntary.

During the presentation of the Department of National Defense’s (DND) budget at the Senate’s plenary session, Cayetano ended his line of questioning to budget sponsor Senator JV Ejercito by addressing the controversy.
Cayetano expressed his frustration, saying that his suggestion was twisted by people who had a grudge against him.

“What I actually said, if those who are able, the richest in the Philippines and the most generous, want to pay their P170,000, wouldn’t it be helpful?” Cayetano said in a mix of English and Filipino.
The minority senator said that he had done some computing and estimated that if the top 1% of the Philippines paid their share of P170,000, it would already result in P200 billion.
Cayetano said that he had also watched news anchors making comments about the suggestion, saying that they should be unbiased and well-researched.

“Ang sabi nila, ‘mahirap na buhay, sakto kang sweldo, bakit sila magbibigay?’. Ang magbibigay yung richest of the rich na gusto, kusa, at generous,” Cayetano said. (They said, ‘Life is hard, the salary is just enough; why would they give?' The ones who would give are the richest of the rich, willful, and generous.)
Cayetano also responded to calls saying that he should contribute first, saying that he has already offered. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Banks may pass on £1.5bn tax rise to customers, warns Bank of England chief
articles.summary: Big lenders will aim to ‘protect their earnings’ amid temporary increase in corporation tax surcharge, says Andrew Bailey

blocks.text: The governor of the Bank of England has warned that banks could look to pass on the £1.5bn cost of Labour’s increase to tax on their profits, a move that would put further pressure on household finances.

John Healey, the chancellor, used his first budget last month to temporarily increase the bank corporation tax surcharge from 3% to 6% for a 15 month period from January, with the proceeds to be used to fund “breathing space” measures for households.

While the level of the increase was less than banks had feared – there had been wide speculation that Healey would reinstate the 8% tax level that was in place until 2023 – the Bank governor, Andrew Bailey, said he would not be surprised if they looked to pass the costs on to customers to “protect their earnings”.

“It’s a market economy, so these are decisions banks will have to take,” Bailey said in an interview with the Times. “You could understand that they will look to pass it on because they will be targeting a rate of return.

“How successful they will be depends on all sorts of things: market conditions, competition within the industry and so on. It wouldn’t be surprising to find out that they will start by trying to do that.”
The JP Morgan chief executive, Jamie Dimon, has said that he intended to find ways to offset the impact of the tax increase on bank profits.
Speaking at an event in London last week, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”.

Healey’s intervention came as households face mounting pressure on finances. This week, the energy regulator for Great Britain said gas and electricity costs will soar by 26% in January, lifting average annual bills to more than £2,000.
House prices fell at their steepest rate in more than three years in October, as potential homebuyers find themselves prices out amid rising mortgage rates.

On Thursday, the Bank of England warned that 6.5 million households are facing higher mortgage costs in the coming years as their deals come up for renewal at significantly higher interest rates.
More than 400,000 UK homeowners will face a monthly increase of £500-a-month over the next three years.
Earlier this month the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee voted to increase the base rate from 3.75% to 4%, the first rise in more than three years.

articles.title: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
articles.summary: More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia has not.

blocks.text: South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.
The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.
Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.
More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

items: In India, growing clamour to criminalise rape within marriage
Marital rape: Delhi high court gives split verdict
India government says criminalising marital rape 'excessively harsh'

blocks.text: Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.
Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.

A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal says. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.
Unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.
"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.
"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."
The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.
In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.
Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.
There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.
But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".

items: India refuses to criminalise marital rape. This new series shines a light on it
India anger as judge frees man accused of raping wife who then died

blocks.text: Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.
"Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal says.
"They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men."
Also a change in law, she says, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.
Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.
In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

articles.title: Sara Duterte admits 'painful small talk' with senators amid OVP budget debates
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte said Friday she had a “painful small talk” with certain senators during her visit to the Senate yesterday for the plenary deliberations on the proposed budget of her…

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 4:10pm

Vice President Sara Duterte said Friday she had a “painful small talk” with certain senators during her visit to the Senate yesterday for the plenary deliberations on the proposed budget of her office for 2027.
Duterte said this in a press conference, stressing that the “national sport” of politicians is pretending to be nice to each other or being two-faced.
“It was a painful small talk… you know, ‘yung pambansang sport ng mga pulitiko is plastikan,” she said.
“So it’s painful when you’re doing it. For me, for others they’re very good at it,” she added.
The Senate on Thursday afternoon swiftly approved the proposed P785.2 million budget of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) for fiscal year 2027.

Duterte was physically present in the Senate session hall when the proposed OVP budget was presented. She was accompanied by OVP chief of staff Zuleika Lopez, OVP Assistant Chief of Staff Lemuel Ortonio, and other officials.
But the Vice President said some of her friends and supporters reacted negatively to her interactions with some lawmakers during her recent Senate visit.
“They’re not happy, marami ang hindi masaya kahapon na mga kaibigan at supporters. Makikita mo ‘yan sa mga group chat ko,” Duterte said.
Asked for her personal reaction, “Ako, I am okay. It was part of my work, I went there for the Office of the Vice President since we need the budget to operate for the year 2027.”
“I don’t have feelings about except that I had to appease many people yesterday because they were not happy with the chitchat,” she added.

The Vice President was seen yesterday interacting with Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian, Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente Sotto III, Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zuburi, and Senate Finance chairman JV Ejercito.
She was also seen talking with known allies Senators Bong Go and Robin Padilla. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Heavy rain, wind and flooding hit much of US on Thanksgiving
articles.summary:
Homes left without power and holiday travel disrupted as storms pound east coast and other parts of the US

Storms have flooded communities in the US east coast, knocking out power to nearly…

blocks.text: Storms have flooded communities in the US east coast, knocking out power to nearly a million customers and prompting the first-ever postponement of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City.

High winds and flooding hammered both coasts, disrupting holiday travel. More than 900,000 homes and businesses were without electricity on Thursday evening, with the majority in east coast states, according to the outage tracking website PowerOutage.us. More than 2,200 flights to or from US destinations were delayed and more than 400 were cancelled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware.
Macy’s postponed the annual Thanksgiving parade until Saturday because of concerns about how the parade’s large balloons would fare in the wind-swept canyons between Manhattan’s skyscrapers.

Torrential rain, high winds and flooding pounded sections of the east coast. New Jersey was under a state of emergency, along with parts of New York. The weather service posted wind advisories from northern Georgia to most of the mid-Atlantic and southern New England.
People were rescued from their cars in New York City because of flooding, said the mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and similar rescues were reported in other coastal communities.
“There is no destination worth your safety,” Mamdani said.

blocks.caption: People walk through a wet midtown Manhattan. Macy's has postponed its Thanksgiving Day parade to Saturday due to weather.   Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty Images

blocks.text: Strong winds and flooding also disrupted train lines, toppled trees and caused power outages on Thanksgiving night, New York City emergency management officials said. Several scaffolding structures collapsed in the wind, with no injuries were reported.
The storms also flooded areas from North Carolina through New Jersey as high tide rolled in. Roads were closed, and emergency workers were rescuing people from cars stranded in water.
Avalon, New Jersey, was seeing some of the worst flooding in its history, said Scott J Wahl, the borough’s business administrator.
“Not quite Hurricane Sandy,” Wahl said of the benchmark storm for his village on the far south end of New Jersey’s Atlantic coast.
Flood waters washed debris over the road, and a few drivers were rescued after driving around barricades into flood waters, but no injuries were reported, Wahl said.
Lance Miller, 54, said flood waters in his Ocean City, New Jersey, neighborhood were about a foot deep and that driving to the nearest supermarket would probably “destroy your car”.
Miller said he would be staying indoors and having Thanksgiving dinner with his wife and daughter. But he said some of his friends were “not so lucky” and had flooding inside their homes.
The Margate City fire department near Atlantic City, New Jersey, posted video on Facebook of water pouring through the city’s streets, even before heavy rains started.
A firefighter said the tide was coming in ferociously, even with an hour to go before its peak. Water closed in on houses, and sandbags were piled in front of businesses.

Some highways and bridges were temporarily closed. The nearly 18-mile (29-km) Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel in southern Virginia was closed for several hours on Thursday morning because of high winds, while NC 12, the only highway connecting Hatteras Island on the North Carolina Outer Banks to the mainland, was closed after seawater breached the dunes and covered the two-lane highway.

blocks.caption: A person walks past the Lincoln Memorial during a rain storm in Washington, DC. Photograph: Anna Rose Layden/Reuters

blocks.text: In Maryland, nearly 2 million water customers in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties were asked to conserve water because of intermittent power disruptions associated with the storm. Baltimore police closed several streets Thursday night after storm surge caused flooding in waterfront neighborhoods.
The storms also prompted several brief tornado warnings on Thursday, including a rare twister south-east of Seattle, Washington.

The US president, Donald Trump, signed a disaster declaration on Thursday for Florida in response to earlier flooding that damaged hundreds of homes and required water rescues. Trump had approved funding earlier this week, but gathered local officials on Thanksgiving to talk about it in a small signing ceremony at his home in West Palm Beach.
Trump was asked about aid for Thursday’s storms on the east coast. “Well, we’re going to look at that. We have some requests from others,” he said.
Heavy snow fell on parts of Illinois and Missouri with St Louis recording 7.3in (18.5cm) of snowfall. Ste Genevieve, Missouri, recorded 14in.
The ice arena in Wentzville, Missouri, which hosts hockey and other ice skating activities, was empty when the roof caved in at about 3 am, according to the city.
Meanwhile, high-tide driven waves and strong winds caused flooding along the Pacific coast on Thursday. The conditions were expected into Friday, according to the National Weather Service.
Record tides along the California coast forced evacuations in areas from Humboldt County in the far north to Ventura County near Los Angeles.
King tides were surging along the west cast.
Video showed a big wave tearing down part of the Pacifica pier in California on Wednesday, sending it into the ocean. Officials had closed the L-shaped pier in the summer after finding cracks.

Amtrak’s Pacific Surfliner posted more than a dozen itinerary changes on social media on Thursday morning, starting with one that said trains could not run through San Clemente “due to track damage”. It also suspended service between Irvine and Oceanside because of washouts caused by high tide conditions. Service was further shut down from San Diego north to Oceanside and up to Los Angeles international airport.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Suan did not propose parliamentary gov’t if VP Sara isn’t impeached
articles.summary: The Cagayan de Oro Press Club also debunked the claim, saying the congressman never made the remarks shown in the altered videos circulating online

blocks.text: Claim: A video shows Cagayan de Oro 1st District Representative Lordan Suan saying that if Vice President Sara Duterte is not impeached, the law should be changed to shift the Philippines into a parliamentary form of government with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. as prime minister.
Why we fact-checked this: Multiple trending posts used a clip of Suan delivering a speech during the Cagayan de Oro Press Club’s 75th Anniversary Gala on November 23.

The video shows Suan supposedly saying, “Kung hindi man ma-impeach si Sara, gumawa na lang tayo ng batas para walang election sa 2028. (If [Vice President] Sara [Duterte] is not impeached, let’s just enact a law to cancel the 2028 elections.) Let’s transform the Philippines into a parliamentary form of government so that President Bongbong Marcos can become prime minister.”
A Facebook page called Defense Lawyers, one of the accounts that posted the video, wrote this as a caption: “Ano daw? BBM as Prime Minister?!!” (Say what? BBM as prime minister?)
The post garnered 11,700 reactions, 4,700 comments, and 1,700 shares as of writing.
Facebook user Amy Ugay also posted a vertical version of the video with a text overlay that says, “Oi Suan ikaw na lang kaya mag prime minister bakit si BBM pa tigilan mo ‘yan kahibangan mo.”
(Hey Suan, why don’t you just become prime minister yourself instead of BBM? Stop this nonsense of yours.)
This post had 2,000 reactions, 742 comments, and 301 shares as of writing.
The facts: The audio used in the video is fake – Suan did not make any statement regarding Duterte, Marcos, or scrapping the elections in 2028.

A video shared by iFM CDO radio station showed Suan’s speech at the event, where he discussed the importance of the press amid widespread misinformation. He also mentioned House Bill No. 9397, or the proposed Right to Information Act, which seeks to institutionalize Filipinos’ right to access information on matters of public concern.
During his four-minute speech, Suan did not mention anything about the elections, Duterte’s impeachment, or proposing the country’s transition to a parliamentary form of government.

Suan’s office also categorically denied the claims, saying in a statement to Rappler on November 27 that the lawmaker remains an advocate of democracy and upholds Filipinos’ right to vote and choose their leaders.
His office added: “Walang puwang sa ating demokrasya ang sinadyang pagpapakalat ng kasinungalingan upang linlangin ang taumbayan.”
(There is no place in our democracy for the deliberate spreading of lies to deceive the public.)

The Cagayan de Oro Press Club refuted the false claims in a Facebook statement published on November 26, clarifying that the congressman joined the event to show solidarity with local journalists and that he never uttered those statements.
“We call on vloggers and netizens to stop spreading unverified information that confuses the public and damages the reputation of our guests,” the statement read further.

articles.title: Digital detoxing: When was the last time you took time off your screens?
articles.summary: Fast-paced media has changed the way we live

blocks.text: There was a time when I realized that I had become more unfocused and forgetful. Whether it’s misplacing my phone or wallet, or needing to take multiple breaks during work, these issues all started occurring more frequently.

I took a step back to understand what had changed. But in fact, nothing changed; I connected my scattered attention to the time I spent on screens and realized what felt like harmless scrolling was starting to spill over into my everyday life.

Doomscrolling in the afternoon or watching movies while eating never seemed like a problem. Still, looking back, it seems like everything that I did always had a digital or auditory companion. Otherwise, every task would feel long, boring, or exhausting. That dependence made me reflect on how my screen time is starting to catch up with me mentally.

This research paper on social media’s impact on the human attention span, published earlier this year, describes my lack of focus and forgetfulness as a result of regular consumption of short-form content. The study suggests that my brain has been wired to feel rewarded by a simple scroll, making activities that require sustained attention feel unrewarding. This becomes problematic when the behavior becomes repetitive, and we begin to use doomscrolling as a way to regulate emotions. Moreover, short-form content was also shown to increase my potential risks of impulsivity, addiction-like behaviors, and depressive symptoms.

Realizing how attached I’ve become to my screen and how it has affected me mentally, I decided to make a change by making two simple promises to refocus and slow down: reduce my screen time by planning my day, and stick to the plan.

Going through a digital detox was one of the most life turning points for me as it shaped a lot of my interests and who I am today. Beyond reducing my time online, it became an act of getting to know myself and finding the right balance of being online and offline.

Finding this balance was the goal of my detox; it involved considering what I did throughout the day and making sure it was a healthy balance I could stick to. I knew simply reducing my screen time wouldn’t work, so I made small daily commitments to activities that would replace my time online.

My first commitment was to take time for physical activity, whether it was a short walk, a run, or a workout; it was my first non-negotiable to do for at least an hour a day. As someone who is already active, I knew it was something I could start with rather than trying to change my entire routine all at once. At first, it was a tiring conscious adjustment I had to keep in mind: tracking my online time and figuring out when and what activity to do. It was a challenging start, but after doing it consistently for a while, it became something that didn’t feel out of the ordinary.

I continued stacking up these commitments, ones that I knew I would enjoy and stick to, such as reading even just a page a day, drawing a simple sketch, learning a new song on the guitar or piano, and taking a short meditation in the morning. They all followed the same strategy: start small, do it every day until it becomes part of the routine, and repeat to the next commitment.

With relationships and work to consider, I knew some days would be too busy for me to follow through on all my commitments, and I allowed myself that flexibility. Detoxing wasn’t a prison I put myself in; it was a way to make room for things that mattered to me, and my relationships and work are part of those. That meant adjusting my commitments around my responsibilities and energy; even if I could only manage a few minutes of an activity or had to skip it for the day, it was all okay. After all, detoxing was an act of self-care for me.

Even though I started this detox a while back, I still find myself sticking to the habits I built. It was a life-changing experience as it taught me how to find a balance between staying connected online and making meaningful time for myself offline. That balance looks different each day, but what mattered to me was being more intentional and mindful about how I spend my time.

Digital detoxing is not a “fix” that could work for everyone. It’s a highly personal journey that you need to commit to that can bring some benefits to your life. What it has done for me is that I have become more mindful of the way I spend my time every day, taught me how to manage my mental health, and most importantly taught me a lot about who I am.

You don’t have to wait until you see signs of excessive digital consumption, as I did. Give it a try, starting with one small, screen-free break in your day. Spend that time doing something you enjoy, and notice how you feel afterward. From there, you can decide which boundaries fit your responsibilities and which habits are worth keeping. – Rappler.com
References:

Masri-zada, T., Martirosyan, S., Abdou, A., Barbar, R., Kades, S., Makki, H., Haley, G., & Agrawal, D. K. (2018). The Impact of Social Media & Technology on Child and Adolescent Mental Health. J Psychiatry Psychiatr Disord. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12165459/

Ramadhan, R. N., Rampengan, D. D., Yumnanisha, D. A., Setiono, S. B., Tjandra, K. C., Ariyanto, M. V., Idrisov, B., & Empitu, M. A. (2024). Impacts of digital social media detox for mental health: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Narra J. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11392003/

articles.title: Wesley So tops Jerusalem Masters, bags P6.4 million
articles.summary: Cavite-born Wesley So captures his fourth chess title this year, saying he plays best when 'ultra relaxed'

blocks.text: NEXT MOVE. Wesley So in action at the 2026 Jerusalem Masters.
Israeli Chess Federation
Cavite-born Wesley So captures his fourth chess title this year, saying he plays best when 'ultra relaxed'

MANILA, Philippines – Filipino-American Super Grandmaster Wesley So notched pulsating back-to-back wins to claim the Jerusalem Masters 2026 title and $101,000 (P6.4 million) late Thursday, November 26, at the Museum of Tolerance in Israel’s capital.

Striking in his last listed major tournament for the year, the Bacoor, Cavite-born So bested Russian Alexey Sarana in the deciding Armageddon for a 3-2 victory in the final of the 12-man all-GM tournament.
They wound up tied after two rapid games and two blitz tiebreakers.
In the semifinal, the 33-year-old So tamed fellow Team USA member Hans Moke Niemann, also via Armageddon when he secured a draw with black.
So clinched his fourth crown this year, including his fourth United States championship, the GCT (Grand Chess Tour) Sinquefield Cup, and the American Cup.
“I’m very happy, no more pressure,” said So in the post-game interview. So disclosed in the semifinals that he plays best when “ultra relaxed” and free from result pressure.

After the round-robin qualifying stage, So was tied with Sarana at 7.0 points, trailing defending champion Arjun Erigaisi, with 9.0 points, and Niemann, with 8.0 points. Russian top seed Ian Nepomniachtchi tallied 6.5 points and missed the knockout semifinals.
It was a remarkable recovery for So, who finished 13th out of 24 participants in last week’s Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest, Hungary.
If any consolation, So fared better than perennial world No. 1 Magnus Carlsen, who landed 17th.
Following his Jerusalem triumph, So gained 10 points and climbed to ninth in the FIDE Live Rapid rating. So is ranked sixth in classical play. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Ombudsman warns public officials against soliciting funds for Christmas parties
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman on Friday warned public officials and employees against using their offices to solicit donations for Christmas parties and other unauthorized purposes.

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 3:46pm
The Office of the Ombudsman on Friday warned public officials and employees against using their offices to solicit donations for Christmas parties and other unauthorized purposes.

The Ombudsman issued the statement following its decision to issue a six-month suspension without pay order against Bayani Galzote Olegario, barangay secretary of Barangay Sta. Cruz, Makati City, over solicitation letters issued using official government letterhead.

The Ombudsman said Olegario issued letters in December 2025 seeking cash or in-kind donations from private individuals for the Christmas party of barangay officials and personnel, making him administratively liable for conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service.

“The Ombudsman found substantial evidence that Olegario's use of his official position, barangay letterhead, and signature to solicit donations tarnished the image and integrity of the barangay government. Using the authority and resources associated with public office to solicit donations for a purpose not established as a government function falls short of the standards of integrity expected of public servants,” the Ombudsman said.

“Such semblance of the imprimatur of public office for a purpose not shown to be a governmental function is inconsistent with the standards of integrity and propriety expected of public employees. It creates the appearance that the government itself is requesting private individuals to provide money or property for the benefit of its personnel,” the Ombudsman added.
Olegario’s conduct, the Ombudsman said, may diminish public confidence in the impartiality and integrity of public service.

“The intended use of the solicitation for a Christmas party did not excuse the conduct, as public officials and employees must not only refrain from corruption and personal enrichment but also avoid invoking the authority of their offices for private or unauthorized purposes,” the Ombudsman said.

If the suspension can no longer be enforced due to separation from service, the penalty shall be converted into a fine equivalent to six months and one day's salary, payable to the Office of the Ombudsman. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Italy's former police chief rejected mafia inquiry allegations before death
articles.summary: The contents of an eight-page letter by Gianni De Gennaro have been revealed days after his body was found at his Tuscany home.

blocks.text: Italian ex-police chief Gianni De Gennaro has denied misleading investigations into high-profile Mafia killings, in a letter written shortly before his death.
His body was found at his Tuscan country home on Saturday and Italian authorities believe he took his own life. A post mortem examination was due to take place on Friday.
In his eight-page note, De Gennaro, 78, vehemently denied obstructing the inquiry into the murder of anti-mafia judge Paolo Borsellino in Sicily in July 1992.
The Cosa Nostra Mafia was found to have ordered Borsellino's killing and that of fellow judge Giovanni Falcone two months earlier.
But several fruitless investigations were later launched into potential cover-ups by high-ranking officials.
In a recent inquiry De Gennaro, who in the 1990s worked in the anti-mafia directorate and later became Italy's police chief, was accused of misdirecting the initial investigation.
The allegations shocked many Italians, as De Gennaro had worked closely with Falcone and was seen as being on the front line of the fight against organised crime.

"In a few minutes I will be gone, so you understand well that a 'man condemned to death' cannot lie," he wrote in the letter, published by Italian daily Corriere della Sera. "I have never betrayed my oath of loyalty to the Fatherland."
"I hope that, amid the avalanche of falsehoods now overwhelming me, the truth will ultimately prevail," he added.
The case, and the media furore that has surrounded it, have re-opened the wound of the Mafia killings of the early 1990s, which remain an emotionally charged issue in Italy.
The story has dominated Italian headlines since De Gennaro's death, with several of the country's most senior political figures publicly commenting on the case.
On Thursday Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she had been "deeply shocked" by the case.
"His words struck us deeply, and I think the most important think we can do now is to help prosecutors who are working to clear things up," she added.
The letter was found next to a hard drive which he said contained notes from his 40-year career.

According to Italian media, investigators seized two hard drives, one from the home of De Gennaro's son and one from a former member of his security detail, and two USB sticks held by a close collaborator, who is also under investigation.
The sticks are reportedly labelled "Stato-Mafia", a likely reference to the alleged relationship between the Italian state and the Mafia, and "Massacres".
Forensic specialists are now expected to examine whether any files on the hard drives or USB sticks were altered or deleted, reports say.
