articles.title: Trend Intel: How the Filipino-inspired Glico Man became a brand mascot blueprint
articles.summary: Before we say goodbye to Osaka’s famous Running Man, we take a deeper look into his history

blocks.text: Before we say goodbye to Osaka’s famous Running Man, we take a deeper look into his history

items: The Glico Man in Osaka is a notable example of a brand mascot that has transcended its original purpose to become a cultural landmark, showcasing the evolving role of mascots in branding and tourism.
Brand mascots, once considered "cringe," are making a comeback, with examples from various industries and countries, including tech companies and food brands.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Hey trendsetters,
“A dancing Jollibee!”

This is what my newfound media friends from different parts of Southeast Asia blurted out when I introduced myself during the Glico Fam Trip, where I was the only representative from the Philippines. All of them gushed about how the Bee’s versions in their respective home countries aren’t as chaotic as the one from back home (I bet they saw those unhinged TikToks).

It’s interesting how their knee-jerk reaction to knowing where I come from is to associate me with a popular fast food chain’s mascot. But even more amusing is to realize how the impact of brand mascots is ultimately having a global resurgence.

Previously “cringe,” brand mascots are now taking over the spotlight (again), said Little Black Book. The Wall Street Journal recently reported a rise in new mascots even from unexpected industries. Tech giants are no exception, with Meta recently unveiling an AI agent called Jolly, who might be intentionally made cute to grow people’s trust amid skepticism. And of course, we can’t deny the massive online impact of Duolingo’s Duo.

blocks.caption: Screenshots from @duolingo on TikTok, showing funny videos of Duo the mascot

blocks.text: Here in the Philippines, we’ve seen Potato Corner’s Poco get its own talking plushie and blind box toys.

In other parts of Asia, Butterbear of Coffee Beans by Dao (Thailand) is a pop culture sensation, Mixue’s Snow King (China) is having an amusement park based on him, and Buldak (South Korea) is introducing a “next-generation character.” The emotion even evolves from love to grief. Take, for example, people’s sentimental reaction to the retirement of Suica, the penguin fronting Japan’s JR East transportation smart card system.

“Mascots work when you need people to remember you even when they’re not paying attention. Children, tired parents, anyone scrolling half asleep. What connects them? Brands that win by being liked, not just respected,” said Jacopo Pesavento, CEO of Branding Records, in Marketing-Interactive.
But if there’s a total hall of famer in the brand mascot department, it would have to be Japan’s Glico Man – the runner almost every Osaka visitor poses with.

Whether you’re taking a well-timed photo in the Dotonbori River or shooting a Reel along with a thick crowd of tourists along the Ebisubashi Bridge with Anri’s I CAN’T STOP THE LONELINESS playing in the background, the Glico Man always makes an appearance, seemingly adding to the major city’s vibrancy.

blocks.caption: People on TikTok posing with the Glico Man as backdrop in different spots

blocks.text: Before its 2014 version with LED lights, the Glico Man was established in 1935 to promote Ezaki Glico’s first product in 1922: A heart-shaped caramel candy with the slogan, “300 metres in a single piece,” implying that this health booster would give you enough energy to run 300 meters.
In case you didn’t know, the Glico Runner is actually inspired by a Filipino. Enter Fortunato Catalon, a track and field legend.

“Not many people know this, but Glico Runner has a Filipino connection. The runner’s pose is said to have been inspired in part by Fortunato Catalon, the Filipino sprinter once celebrated as Asia’s fastest man, together with two Japanese runners – marathon pioneer Shizo Kanakuri and top sprinter Sasago Tani,” said a representative from Glico Philippines.

These days, Osaka tourists are “last chance rushing” their way to Glico Man’s photo spots. The multinational confectionery company announced that the iconic sign will be covered starting December 1, as it’s up for a revamp, marking its seventh redesign since 1935. Don’t fret, as the runner will remain and is planned to be unveiled by spring (approximately March to May) in 2027.

How people on TikTok are documenting their final sight at the landmark is testament enough to the Running Man’s impact as a brand mascot – it no longer just represents a brand, but has already become synonymous with an entire city.

The brand mascot to cultural landmark pipeline rarely happens, but when it does, it’s pretty worth it. In this case, a successful brand mascot is one that acts on its own, without needing constant deliberate action from its creators, as the audience has already become a huge player in promoting it through organic user-generated content. Plus, the accessibility it offers has allowed it to become an unofficial tourist spot.

We may chalk this phenomenon up to the “kidult” economy or people’s sudden drive to add whimsy to their mundane lives. But this interesting era of brand mascot renaissance in the age of AI may ultimately remind us that we might just need something overwhelmingly physical to see – or maybe even touch.
Which brand mascot pulled you in recently? Share your stories (or photos!) with us.
Until the next scroll!
Jelou Galang
Culture Desk Content Producer

articles.title: Grace Tame calls out ex-Murdoch media executive who said she ‘must be looking to be raped again’
articles.summary:
Matt Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch, admits making offensive remark and says he was referencing assault survivor’s ‘strikingly attractive get-up’

  • Get our

blocks.text: A former Murdoch media executive has admitted he said Grace Tame “must be looking to be raped again” at an event, after the former Australian of the year overheard the comment and confronted him.

Tame, a child sexual assault victim survivor who was Australian of the year in 2021 for her advocacy work, revealed in an opinion piece for Crikey that she heard Matt Handbury make the comment to another man at a function last week.
“That’s Grace Tame. Look at her with her tits hanging out. She must be looking to be raped again,” Handbury said, according to Tame’s piece published on Friday.
Tame wrote that she didn’t realise that the man was Handbury until a bystander told her. He introduced himself as “Matt” after she confronted him.
The 77-year-old is Rupert Murdoch’s nephew and the former owner of Murdoch Magazines and Murdoch Books. He is now on the board of The Sydney Retreat, a rehab centre.
Tame said Handbury conceded at the UNSW event – where former military lawyer David McBride was presented with an award – that he had made the comment.
The following day, Handbury sent an email to Tame, seen by Guardian Australia, in which he also admitted he said “she must be looking to be raped again”.

Tame was 15 when repeatedly sexually abused by her 58-year-old maths teacher, Nicolaas Bester, who was later convicted and jailed. In 2019, Tame won a supreme court exemption which overturned a Tasmanian law that had until then gagged her from speaking about her experiences of assault.
“He didn’t say she must be looking to get raped,” Tame said of Handbury’s comment.
“He said she must be looking to get raped again. Therefore evidencing his prior knowledge of what I have been through.”
Tame said that the comment “activated really deep seated trauma and there are consequences to that”.
“It’s really destabilising and disorienting because your body is essentially your abused self and it is in total survival mode,” she said.

Handbury said in the email to Tame: “I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up. It was meant to be in appreciation in a male-to-male exchange. I can see that might be offensive in the context of suggesting a woman is making herself attractive to men in some titillating fashion.”

“I also said: ‘She must be looking to be raped again.’ This was certainly meant for no one’s ears but my friend. However it was in poor taste. In fact in highly objectionable taste and I regretted it as soon as I got out into the fresh air. Thank you for calling me out.

“Some men, obviously including myself, are prone to finding suggestive humour in the wrong places. I deeply regret my letting such bad habits get in the way of common courtesy, respect and decency. Please accept my humblest apologies.

“Thank you for opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink on Friday. But no one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous that night.”
‘I’m tired of the maltreatment’

Tame wrote in her Crikey piece that “what makes this provocation especially egregious is that Matt didn’t reference an imagined harm, but a very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about”.
after newsletter promotion
“It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?” she wrote.
“This isn’t about Matt personally; it’s about a broader culture of normalised violence. However, part of that culture is the self-censorship that protects people like him.”

Tame referred to research that showed 35% of Australian men believe women’s rights have come too far, adding that “research has repeatedly shown that misogynistic attitudes are a broad predictor of violent extremism and prevalent among men of all ages.”
Tame told Guardian Australia she often faced re-traumatising behaviour from men.
“I’m tired. I’m tired of the maltreatment. I’m tired of the gaslighting. I’m tired of being baited and then have people be shocked why I would be angry or re-traumatised,” she said on Friday.
Tame thanked bystanders at the event who supported her following Handbury’s comment.
The chief executive of Full Stop Australia, Karen Bevan, called on people to speak up if they heard similar comments because “we all have the power to shift this”.

“If one of the most recognised survivor advocates in the country can be spoken about like this at an event honouring a whistleblower in a room full of people, you can be assured this behaviour is normalised,” Bevan said.
“Things like this do get said in workplaces, pubs, group chats and boardrooms across the country, where no one is recording, and no one writes about it afterwards.”
Handbury was contacted for comment, as was The Sydney Retreat.

articles.title: Marcos urged anew: Declare El Niño state of calamity
articles.summary: Senator Francis Pangilinan on Friday urged President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. anew to declare a state of calamity over the El Niño phenomenon to address budgeting shortfalls.

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 2:50pm
Senator Francis Pangilinan on Friday urged President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. anew to declare a state of calamity over the El Niño phenomenon to address budgeting shortfalls.

Pangilinan issued the statement during budget deliberations of the Department of Agriculture (DA) at the Senate. The DA and its attached agencies are asking for P203.56 billion for 2027, with Pangilinan serving as the budget sponsor in the upper chamber.
Senator Risa Hontiveros said 4.3 million farmers and fisherfolk are estimated to be affected by the El Niño phenomenon.
She asked Pangilinan how many of the affected farmers and fisherfolk would be able to receive aid or cash for work.
Citing data from the DA, Pangilinan said a P5-billion budget has been allotted for these sectors. From their ranks, 1.67 million farmers and fisherfolk could benefit from a P3,000-cash assistance.

The DA is also working with the Department of Social Welfare and Development and the Department of Labor and Employment for additional welfare programs. Rice farmers under the Rice Competitiveness Enhancement Fund will get P6 billion.
Pangilinan admitted that it is not enough.

"We are calling on the President to declare that state of national emergency calamity because as of November 2026, the calamity fund, disaster fund, is about P112 billion, so the response of Malacañang if I recall correctly is 'not yet,'" Pangilinan said.

"So, ibig sabihin (So, that means), they intend to, at the right time, but I'd like to think that the right time should be soon. Considering we don't want it to get worse before it gets worst. So that assistance is really necessary," he added.

Pangilinan added that Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. agreed that the declaration was needed to address the shortfall in the funding for 4.3 million farmers and fisherfolk affected by El Niño.
GMA News has reached out to Malacañang for comment, but it has yet to respond as of posting time.

Senators, through Senate Resolution 765, collectively called on the President earlier this month to declare a state of calamity under the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act in areas affected or threatened by the El Niño.

Under the law, a state of calamity would allow the President to impose price ceilings on basic necessities. Government or lending institutions may also grant non-interest loans to affected populations. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: AirAsia PH says flights unaffected as DOLE vows to avert pilots' strike
articles.summary: AirAsia Philippines said its flights would operate as scheduled, a day after its pilots' union filed a notice of strike over the airline's plan to lay off about 90 pilots.

blocks.text: November 27, 2026 | 2:43pm
Airplanes are seen at Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) on March 18, 2026.
STAR / Walter Bollozos

MANILA, Philippines — AirAsia Philippines said on Friday, November 27, its flights would operate as scheduled, a day after its pilots' union filed a notice of strike over the airline's plan to lay off about 90 pilots.

"AirAsia Philippines remains fully operational and committed to serving the Philippine market," general manager and president Anna Victoria Lu said in a statement. "We want to assure our passengers that the announced workforce adjustment will not affect their flight, booking, or other services."
Lu said the airline's domestic and international flights would operate on schedule, and that check-in, boarding and customer support would continue as usual.

She described the job cuts as "a difficult decision we made to support the long-term stability of the airline amid sustained cost pressures," and said the company was committed to supporting affected employees and their families.
In announcing the cuts on Thursday, Lu blamed high jet fuel prices and unfavorable exchange rates.

Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino said on Thursday, November 26, that the Department of Labor and Employment had convened the National Conciliation and Mediation Board, the agency that handles strike notices and mediates between employers and unions, to take up the dispute.

"We are giving this issue top priority because it concerns the transport, airline, and aviation industry," Tolentino told reporters on the sidelines of the 14th Gawad Kaligtasan at Kalusugan National Awarding Ceremony in Quezon City. "I will personally oversee this to ensure that travelers' journeys are not delayed."

articles.title: ‘Absolute jerk’: police investigating after 500-year-old ‘King Jarrah’ tree chainsawed in WA national park
articles.summary:
Western Australian authorities are scrambling to save the ‘iconic’ 36-metre tree in Wellington national park south of Perth

  • Get our

blocks.text: Western Australian authorities say they are considering “all options” in their race to save a beloved jarrah tree they suspect was vandalised with a chainsaw in a national park south of Perth.
Police on Friday said they were treating the vandalism of “King Jarrah” as an alleged criminal damage incident, as they appealed to the public to help them find the person or people responsible.
The tree, in Wellington national park near Bunbury, was damaged on 21 or 22 November when someone attempted to cut it down, police said.
The WA environment minister, Matt Swinbourn, said an “absolute jerk” had damaged the “iconic” tree with a chainsaw, in an act he described as “appalling, senseless, and heartbreaking”.

“It’s hard to fathom how shocking it is that someone would do this to a tree believed to be about 500 years old, particularly in a national park,” he said in a statement on social media on Thursday night.
“Western Australians love this tree. Our community will be heartbroken, and they have every right to be angry.”

blocks.caption: The WA environment minister said an ‘absolute jerk’ had allegedly damaged the jarrah tree with a chainsaw. Photograph: Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA)

blocks.text: Experts, including an independent specialist arborist, were assessing the tree’s condition, but the immediate priorities were giving it every possible chance of survival and finding those responsible, Swinbourn said.
“Whoever did this has damaged something precious to all of us,” he said.
Swinbourn said surveillance cameras have been installed in the area, which had been closed to the public.
“If you know anything, come forward,” he said. “Anyone capable of such a deliberate and callous act should be held accountable.”
after newsletter promotion
The jarrah tree, Eucalyptus marginata, is a towering hardwood native found only in the forests of south-west WA, which plays a vital role in the local ecosystem.
Visitors travel to the state to see the jarrahs, known for their towering foliage and longevity, as well as their rich red timber and honey.
The state’s biodiversity, conservation and attractions department said a member of the public reported the damage to the parks and wildlife service on Tuesday.

A chainsaw had been used around the base of the tree, one of the tallest in the national park at 36 metres, which is the “focus and drawcard” of a small day-use recreation site, the spokesperson said.
They said a consultant arborist and relevant government staff travelled to the national park on Wednesday to assess the health and safety of the tree.
Formal technical advice from the consultant arborist on whether King Jarrah could be saved was expected next week, they said.
“All options are being considered to save this iconic tree,” the spokesperson said.

They said vandalism of this nature was a potential breach of several sections of the Conservation and Land Management Act 1984 and, if found guilty, court penalties for the person or people responsible could include a fine of up to $10,000 and one year’s imprisonment.
Police said a silver Jeep was seen in the area in the days after the incident and they believed whoever was in the car may be able to assist with their inquiries.
They encouraged anyone with information to contact them via crime stoppers.

articles.title: EU leaders fail to bridge budget splits as talks stall
articles.summary: Aid for Ukraine was among the disputes as EU members hope to conclude talks by the end of the year.

blocks.text: European Union (EU) leaders have deferred negotiations on its long-term budget after tensions surfaced over the bloc's spending priorities and aid for Ukraine.
Tense talks on the 2028-34 budget ended after 12 hours on Thursday at a summit in Brussels, with some members walking out of negotiations that will resume in December.

Divisions were largely split along the lines of countries, including France and Italy, wanting to approve a higher-spending proposal against those advocating for financial restraint, with Germany chief among them.
Many members want the budget locked in ahead of several high-stakes elections held across Europe in 2027, including in France.
Countries remain divided over a proposal to provide Ukraine with an additional loan of €45bn (£37.6bn), split between non-military and military funding.
Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary have objected to the loan, but German Chancellor Frederich Merz said uniform EU agreement was a condition for approving the broader budget.
"I stand by my view that aid for Ukraine must be supported by the European Union as a whole," Merz told reporters.
"The European Union comprises of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."

Bulgaria, which previously opposed the plan, said it would agree to fund part of the loan that commits non-military financial support to Kyiv, marking a small sign of progress emerging from the special summit of the European Council.
EU members have been wrangling over the long-term budget after the European Commission submitted a €2tn proposal earlier this year, with some countries objecting to high levels of spending.
Those advocating higher spending want the funds to future-proof industries such as farming and invest in regional development. Fiscally cautious countries want to avoid amassing ballooning debt.
Thursday's talks were set up by the European Council to unblock the impasse, with a proposal to reduce spending by approximately €220bn to €230bn.
Under the current proposal, the budget totals €1.582tn, which includes €140bn to repay pandemic-era borrowing.
Four countries wanting to rein in the budget, including Denmark and Austria, walked out of negotiations after several hours of meetings.

Merz said there was "new movement" towards reducing the size of the EU budget, though he added "we are not there yet" when he confirmed that a new round of negotiations would not take place in Brussels on Friday.
European budgets requires approval from all 27 countries, with each country effectively holding veto power.
French President Emmanuel Macron said it would be a "strategic mistake" to lower long-term spending.

France's forthcoming presidential election came into focus during the EU budget talks, with frontrunner Marine Le Pen calling the talks an "underhanded political manoeuvring to thwart the democratic will of the French people".
Last month, Le Pen announced she would significantly reduce French aid to Ukraine and EU contributions if she were to win the presidency.

Macron addressed Le Pen's remarks on the sidelines of the Brussels summit, saying: "It is an odd kind of arrogance to behave as if she is already in charge of France's destiny because, as things stand, she has not been elected."
Once the talks concluded, the European Council announced a two-day summit on 17 and 18 December would revive budget negotiations.
Spanish economist Pablo Hernández de Cos was also named as the next President of the European Central Bank, replacing Christine Lagarde from February 2027.

articles.title: Houthi attacks test Saudi Arabia's image of security
articles.summary: Despite the strikes, markets and restaurants in Riyadh remain busy as residents express trust in the government to protect them.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Houthis said they were responsible for an attack on an oil facility south of Riyadh on 3 October, one of a growing number
ByNawal Al-Maghafi
Senior international investigations correspondentReporting fromRiyadh
Ten days after fleeing his home in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, Abu Khalil is selling socks on the streets of Riyadh.
"I walked out of Sanaa, I crossed the front line," he says, adding that he "hitched a ride into Saudi Arabia".
Families in Yemen are "struggling to provide for [their] children", he says, as he tries to earn enough to send some money home.

He asks us not to use his full name because his wife and four children are still in Sanaa, and he is frightened of what might happen to them if he is identified speaking out against the Houthis. "I ran away from the Houthis but I couldn't bring my family with me. May God protect them," he says.

Backed by Iran, the armed group has controlled much of northern Yemen since a civil war erupted more than a decade ago. It is fighting the internationally recognised government, which is supported by neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
And Saudi cities, such as Riyadh, are now coming under regular drone and missile attacks from the very group Abu Khalil fled.

An informal ceasefire in Yemen unravelled in July, and since the fighting escalated, the Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia. They have said they were retaliating against deadly Saudi air strikes in Yemen and what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory.
One Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured more than 300 - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Surveillance footage shows the moment of the attack at King Khalid International Airport on 10 October

blocks.text: Image source, Saudi Ministry of Media/Reuters
Surveillance footage shows the moment of the attack at King Khalid International Airport on 10 October

Having been granted rare permission to report from Riyadh, we spoke to locals, including Majid, a 25-year-old engineer who works for the Saudi state oil company Aramco. He was passing through the airport that day, rushing for a flight to Jeddah for a religious pilgrimage.
He says he was watching a mother push her children in a pushchair when the terminal was hit.
He remembers seeing a man covered in blood. "I went to him in shock, asking him, 'Are you OK?'" He says he saw injured and unconscious passengers being taken to the airport's first aid clinic.
"Some of them, I still don't know whether they were alive or not."
The experience left him shaken. "The threat is real," he tells me. "But I will not let the Houthis make me feel unsafe in my own country."

The airport attack was far from an isolated incident. BBC analysis of data from the US-based Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled), a non-profit organisation, which collects data on political violence and protests around the world, identified 274 attacks on Saudi Arabia in almost five months between 1 July and 25 November.
According to Acled, most of these were intercepted, but at least 41 were not and in some cases debris from the interception also caused damage.
Drones featured in almost two-thirds of the attacks, while ballistic missiles were used in more than half, according to the data.
In the previous five months, Acled recorded just one Houthi attack on the country.
Backed by Iran, the Houthis have developed an increasingly sophisticated arsenal, dramatically extending their ability to repeatedly strike deep in Saudi territory.

blocks.caption: Map showing the location of Saudi Arabia with Yemen to the south, the Red Sea to the west and Iran across the Gulf to the east. Sanaa, Taiz and Aden are marked in south-west Yemen. Riyadh is roughly in the middle of Saudi Arabia with Dammam to its east and Medina to its west.

blocks.text: For years, Houthi attacks were largely concentrated near the Yemeni border, with Riyadh targeted far less frequently. But since the collapse of the unofficial ceasefire, the Saudi capital, more than 700km (430 miles) away from the Yemeni border, is now coming under regular attack.
As well as the airport, oil installations and prominent buildings in the capital have been in danger.

Saudi Arabia has spent billions transforming its cities, attracting international investment and presenting itself to the world as a safe place to live, work and visit - the attacks have put this promise to the test.
Two prominent skyscrapers have been hit in Riyadh's financial district this month.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Saudi Arabia's tallest skyscraper, the PIF tower, was struck on 19 November

blocks.text: Image source, Saudi Press Agency/Reuters
Saudi Arabia's tallest skyscraper, the PIF tower, was struck on 19 November

Eleven people were injured in a strike on the Public Investment Fund (PIF) Tower, which is the tallest in Saudi Arabia and is the headquarters of the country's sovereign wealth fund. The other was the Aramco building, home to the state oil company.
As we drove past the Aramco tower, the damage was a clear reminder of the threat facing the kingdom.

But within days, the building's exterior had been completely repaired, any visible sign of the attack erased. It was perhaps a reflection of Saudi Arabia's determination to project an image of stability and business as usual, even as the attacks continue.
The government has condemned "terrorist attacks targeting civilian and economic facilities" and said it would "take all necessary measures" to defend itself.
Even so, flights to the capital have been severely disrupted by the strikes, which have also targeted other locations, such as Medina and the airport in the eastern city of Dammam.
Many passengers travelling to Riyadh are being routed through different airports and making the final leg of the journey on land.
The flight we took to Dammam was almost empty. Riyadh's streets tell a different story, though.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Stallholders in Riyadh's markets are trading as normal

blocks.text: Image source, BBC/Liam Weir
Stallholders in Riyadh's markets are trading as normal
Restaurants are bustling, families browse at shopping centres and people go about their evenings seemingly undeterred by the threat overhead.
But getting people to speak openly about the conflict is difficult in a country where strict censorship laws and restrictions on freedom of expression make many wary of talking to the media.

Many of those who did speak to us expressed confidence in their country's ability to protect them. At a busy market, Badr says the airport attack was worrying, but life has quickly returned to normal. "I sleep comfortably," he says, praising the country's security forces.
Another man, Rashid, gestures towards the stalls around us: "The market is booming. People are buying and selling, going about their business. Everything is good."

But the normality he describes is periodically disturbed by a sudden buzz on the phone with an alert warning of an incoming attack. Then come the loud booms of air defences intercepting missiles and drones overhead.
We experienced one at 04:00 one morning, and the knowledge that not every attack is being intercepted can leave people afraid.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Alex Malouf says the attacks and alerts can be hard for children to deal with

blocks.text: Alex Malouf says the attacks and alerts can be hard for children to deal with

British expatriate Alex Malouf, who has lived in Saudi Arabia on and off since 2006, says he worries about the psychological impact on his 11-year-old daughter, who has experienced security alerts while at school.
"There have been times when my daughter has said, 'Daddy, I'm scared.' It has been something which I think has shaken our reality."
Despite the attacks, Abu Khalil says he feels much safer in Saudi Arabia than at home in Yemen where fighting has intensified.

The Houthis' renewed offensive in western Yemen has seen the group capture territory along the Red Sea coast and threaten strategic routes towards the southern city of Aden, the government's temporary base.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The wreckage of a shoe factory following a Saudi-led strike on Sanaa on 17 November

blocks.text: Image source, EPA/Shutterstock
The wreckage of a shoe factory following a Saudi-led strike on Sanaa on 17 November
The fighting has also intensified around Taiz, a government-controlled city that has endured years of siege and conflict.

Road closures resulting from the latest Houthi siege there have severely restricted deliveries of essential supplies, leaving more than 800,000 people cut off from humanitarian assistance, according to the UN children's agency Unicef. Food and fuel that can be found have shot up in price.

More than 360,000 people have been forced from their homes in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). And the UN Human Rights Office has verified 323 civilian casualties since then, including 76 killed, with children accounting for half of the dead.

A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has responded to the Houthi advances and attacks on the kingdom with intensified air strikes, adding to the dangers faced by civilians. One strike in Sanaa earlier this month killed 44 people, according to Houthi authorities. Saudi Arabia says these operations were to protect the Yemeni population and global trade from the Houthis.
Saudi-led bombing campaigns during the earlier years of the war killed thousands of civilians and devastated homes, hospitals and schools.
The Houthis have also inflicted enormous suffering on civilians through shelling, missile and ground attacks on government-held territory, as well as repression in areas under their control.
Abu Khalil hopes that he will soon be able to bring his wife and children over to Saudi Arabia, away from the dangers in Sanaa, and says he "will not go back until the Houthis are gone".
Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer and Ahmed Nour

articles.title: Leaders clash in final Spain election debate as housing dominates run-in
articles.summary: The struggle many face in buying a home has been the biggest issue of a bitter campaign.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Jangling keys has turned into a symbol of protest against Spain's housing struggles
ByNick Beake
Europe correspondentReporting fromValencia
Spain's main party leaders have made their last pitch to voters in a fractious final TV debate that focused heavily on the country's housing crisis.
Spaniards go to the ballot box on Sunday, with opinion polls suggesting Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will fail to extend his eight years in office.

The debate on Thursday night marked the culmination of a campaign, which has been defined by the din of house keys being jangled in symbolic protest, rather than any carefully crafted words of politicians.
The struggle many face in opening the door to an affordable home has led to demonstrations filling plazas across the country.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo of the conservative People's Party (PP), who is poised to replace Sánchez, told viewers he would build a million new homes.
The PP, which is narrowly projected to be the largest party, is poised to form a government with the Vox party which is polling in third place.
If Vox do win a share of power at a national level, it would be the first time for the far right in Spain's 50 years of democracy since Francisco Franco's dictatorship.
Vox's leader Santiago Abascal told the debate only he cared about those who had the greatest housing need.
Ada Colau, who heads a left-wing coalition of four small left-wing parties called Broad Front, said taxing rich and exploitative landlords was urgently required.
Rejecting criticism that he had failed to tackle the country's housing problem, Sanchez talked up his recent emergency measures designed to protect tenants and cap rents.

Sparking the protests in September was the eviction – and subsequent death in hospital – of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal (no relation to Santiago). She could not afford a tripling of her rent in Madrid.
But it is Spain's third city, Valencia, that is at the heart of what many call a full-blown housing crisis.
"We want to live together but we look at the prices of property and it's impossible," says 25-year-old Nuria Cifuentes from the city.
She and her boyfriend Miguel Martínez work as sports journalists but are still living with their respective families because of the high cost of renting a flat, even with their combined salaries.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Nuria and Miguel want to live together but feel they are priced out

blocks.text: Nuria and Miguel want to live together but feel they are priced out
"Half of what we earn would go on rent of more than €1,000 a month," Miguel, 26, says.
We meet the couple outside Valencia's futuristic science museum, whose distinctive design is often compared to the skeleton of a whale.
This coastal location has witnessed the biggest rise in rent prices of any major Spanish city over the past half a decade, according to official data from the INE, the national statistics office.
One study from the city's Polytechnic University put the increase at 78% between 2020 and 2025.
Sánchez called a snap election after Congress rejected his emergency housing reforms.

A revised version was later pushed through a parliamentary standing committee – restricting evictions and capping rent rises – but opponents say he has had eight years to sort the problem and has resolutely failed.
Nuria and Miguel say the soaring cost of housing means that life is on pause for them, as they're unable to make concrete plans for the future.
"Maybe we want to have kids, maybe we want to actually buy somewhere, but there are so many unknowns that all I see is a black expanse," Nuria says.
"The problem here is that our salaries are very low and life is very expensive."
The wider cost of living is the second most important issue for Spaniards, according to numerous surveys carried out during this election period.

Wages failing to catch up with rising prices – despite Spain's GDP growing faster than the three bigger EU countries, Germany, France and Italy – is another reason why Sánchez's PSOE party is only sitting in second place, according to final opinion polls.
Feijóo is said to be most likely to form the next government with the support of Vox under its leader Santiago Abascal.
Having called access to housing a "vital emergency", Feijóo wants to cut taxes for under-40s buying their first home and scrap the Socialists' housing law.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Pedro Sánchez (left) and Núñez Feijóo on screen during the leaders' debate

blocks.text: Image source, Europa Press via Getty Images
Pedro Sánchez (left) and Núñez Feijóo on screen during the leaders' debate
On housing, Vox has gone further than PSOE and PP, promising to prioritise Spaniards over foreigners for social housing and housing aid, as well as other welfare benefits.

On immigration, identified as the third most important issue, Vox advocates deportations for criminals from abroad and, most controversially, a policy of remigration for foreign nationals who "do not contribute to Spain".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Daniel, 30, is unemployed and says he is ready to vote for Vox for the first time

blocks.text: Daniel, 30, is unemployed and says he is ready to vote for Vox for the first time
Opponents of Vox say those who have arrived legally and live and work peacefully risk being forced out.
But 30-year-old Daniel, who is currently unemployed, says he is ready to give his vote to Vox for the first time.
"First of all, it's immigration. It's bad in Spain today – that's why I'm going further to the right," he says.
"The left helps those who don't work, but we need people who work and contribute. We need to give less aid to people who come from abroad and don't contribute."
Daniel says taxes need to come down immediately.
"We are almost being charged to just breathe at the moment," he says.
We meet Daniel coming out of a shopping centre. We explain that other people we met in the previous hour who told us they support Vox did not want to give their name or be photographed.
Is he proud to be voting far right, or does he have concerns about his choice?
"I'll say it like it is… I've always been centre right but have gone to the extreme right… I've decided to choose nationalism."
Spain's control of its borders was criticised by 22 of its 26 EU partners in the summer, in a rebuke to Sánchez.
In July more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory of Ceuta in just two days.
Vox called it an "invasion".
Sánchez has argued the foreign workforce is essential to Spain's economic growth, and in April announced plans to give half a million undocumented migrants legal status.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Maria and German feel they have little choice but to back the Socialist party

blocks.text: Maria and German feel they have little choice but to back the Socialist party

In the final days of the campaign, Sánchez has made a flurry of new spending announcements amounting to billions of euros, promising wage rises in the public sector, higher pensions and discounted transport.
Twenty-year-old student María García says she welcomes the promises but asks why they have come so late in the day.

"The Socialist party have been in power for eight years and now suddenly, during the election campaign, they are passing a lot of progressive laws – which I agree with – but isn't that hypocritical?" she says.
"I don't really have a choice but to vote for them, but come on – you had eight years to do all this!"
Maria's sentiments chime with those of her boyfriend German Martinez, 18.
I put it to them that nearly a fifth of Spaniards are said to be choosing Vox and a number of studies say it's set to be the top choice of first-time voters.
María shakes her head.
"I believe Spain is stepping into the lion's den because we are scared of the dogs outside. We need to be careful," she says.
"People need to inform themselves – just listen to what these guys say. That 20% of Spanish people agree with them really scares me."
Sánchez will be hoping that fear among the undecided of a national government that includes Vox will save him.
He is a great political survivor, but even if his party wins the most votes he has no obvious path to build a majority.
The man who called a snap election over housing now faces his own eviction - from office.
More on Spain's election

articles.title: Mad about mara: the DIY dance movement helping young Nigerians escape the daily grind
articles.summary:
What started as one artist’s response to being cut out of a music video has exploded, becoming a driving force in Nigeria’s cultural landscape

As a student in the central Nigerian city of…

blocks.text: As a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.

In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent.
“I was in a restaurant and everybody was anticipating seeing me, but my face did not show once,” the 27-year old, known as DJ Khalipha, said. “I felt disgraced. I stopped posting the song.”

blocks.caption: Lawal Habeeb Kola, aka DJ Khalipha. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: Khalipha retreated to his dorm and revisited the DIY “cruise beats” genre of dance music that he had previously worked in. Taking its name from the pidgin expression “catch cruise”, meaning to joke around, cruise beats is a lo-fi, frenetic genre that incorporates amusing voice samples from Nollywood and memes.

Khalipha raised the already fast 115-120 beats per minute of cruise beats to 140-150bpm, added melancholic undertones and named the new style mara, meaning to lose one’s senses. The popularity of the sound soared, eventually crossing over from the Lagos underground and becoming incorporated into the sound of mainstream musicians.

As the genre exploded, Khalipha lost creative control. “It became a trend that every producer and DJ was hopping on,” said Feranmi Abiola, 24, who directed the 2025 documentary Mara Mania. “They were making sounds and whether it was mara sound or not, they would just title it mara fever, mara this, mara that.”

Like its predecessors, mara’s spread was driven by choreography. One dancer, Obi “Odogwu Mara” Madubogwu, named himself after the sound and dropped dance routines on social media weekly, gaining street credibility. His death in unclear circumstances at the age of 26 galvanised interest in mara, especially among young Nigerians for whom posting and responding to dance challenges in his style became a form of escape from poor job prospects in Nigeria’s sluggish economy.

blocks.caption: Mara producer Azzi On The Beat, left, and his manager, Kadima. Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The Guardian

blocks.text: “We’ve seen area boys [street urchins] switching to become dancers,” said the producer Azzi On The Beat, an early adopter of mara who has stayed true to the sound. “The music is spiritual.”

The hectic but harmonious sound has become a fixture at raves, which in Nigeria take the form of street-style block-gatherings populated by young people tired of the markup on alcohol at nightclubs and “bottle culture” – the buying of expensive bottles of champagne and spirts in VIP sections, often as a means of flaunting wealth.
Top musicians have been enlisting the sound in search of new hits, but mara’s originators remain relatively unknown, their work often restricted to the thriving underground “TrenchTok” scene.
Khalipha said bookers assumed that mara DJs would have an air of chaos and violence, due to the raw sound of the music and its association with street culture.

Abiola agreed. “[Mara DJs] are not harmful, but they face stereotypes because of their background, how they look and how they dress,” she said. “In my documentary, I wanted people to see these people for who they were … young people innovating and contributing to the cultural identity of this generation. Regardless of where they are from, they deserve to be taken seriously.”
after newsletter promotion

Without institutional backing, the DJs have been learning how to navigate the music industry on the go. When the samples they were using were flagged for copyright issues, they created their own instrumentals from scratch using plugins.

Many artists are self-funded, investing money earned as social media influencers or from royalties into shooting videos and promotion. Female dancers talk of sexual harassment and financial exploitation in the industry.
“The financial challenges are more apparent for the dancers, because people don’t really take dancers seriously,” said Abiola.

Pointing to a square littered with weeds and rubbish, where goats roamed next to a woman sieving black-eyed peas on a tray, Azzi’s 27-year-old manager, Sangokunle Anuoluwapo – known as Kadima – said: “We do most of our videos here.”

Despite the challenges, the people involved in mara harbour dreams of global traction. Support from the French embassy helped Azzi perform at festivals in Uganda and parts of Europe. A few industry friends on the rise or those who Kadima at one point managed also help intermittently with funding or promoting projects for free.
“I understand what we want for this culture so we keep pushing really hard,” said Kadima. “It’s family work, so we try to split revenues among everybody.”

Azzi was given a leg up from the Footprints of David Art Academy, a children’s dance theatre troupe that held performances behind his mother’s shop. He honed his dancing skills, learned how to drum, and met Kadima there. “We were taught how to fight through tough times,” Azzi said.

The art director Seun Awobajo launched the academy in 2005 with the aim of channelling the energy of disadvantaged children into creative endeavours. “[I had] the notion that no child is useless, they are only used less,” he said.

Awobajo is proud of his former wards and the mara scene more generally. “Being proud is an understatement,” he said. “But I think I feel more fulfilled seeing what they’ve become because these are children who the upper class of the society have written off.”

articles.title: Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson launches last-ditch High Court appeal
articles.summary: Erin Patterson is serving life in prison for poisoning her relatives with a toxic mushroom lunch in 2023.

blocks.text: Australia's mushroom killer Erin Patterson has launched a final legal bid to overturn her murder convictions and avoid dying in jail.
Erin Patterson, 52, was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023.

Last month, in Victoria's Court of Appeal three judges dismissed an appeal against her convictions and threw out the possibility she could be released on parole – saying her crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms".
She has now made a last-ditch application to the High Court to look at her case.
Patterson had 28 days to file an application for special leave to appeal to the High Court, a deadline which expired on Friday.
She wants the country's top judges to examine both her conviction and sentence - but the court does not have to agree to look at the case. It only hears appeals in about 10% of cases.

After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms which she had tracked down, foraged and prepared.
Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.
He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.

Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.

Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face. This glimmer of hope of freedom was thrown out by the appeal judges, who ruled she should never be released.
She had argued her conviction was unsafe on seven grounds - including a hotel booking mix up which saw the jury stay in the same place as the prosecution, a key police witness and the media.
Her lawyers said this was "catastrophic" and undermined the integrity of her trial, but the appeal court judges dismissed all the grounds for appeal.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Photos of Duterte in the hospital are AI-generated
articles.summary: The viral posts, claiming to show photos of a bedridden Duterte, circulated ahead of his ICC trial. No official reports confirm his alleged hospitalization.

blocks.text: Claim: Former president Rodrigo Duterte was taken to the hospital ahead of the start of his trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC), as shown in photos circulating online.
Why we fact-checked this: A collage of images depicting an individual resembling Duterte lying in a hospital bed has circulated on Facebook since November 24.

On November 25, Facebook user “Atty. Shiela Sison” shared the collage in a post that garnered 2,900 reactions, 926 comments, and 61 shares as of writing. The page “Sen. Rodante Marcoleta Supporters” posted it a day earlier, receiving 699 reactions, 126 comments, and 10 shares as of writing.
Both posts use the caption: “Get well soon po Tatay Digong sinugod sa hospital matapos…”
(Get well soon, Father Digong. Rushed to the hospital after…)

The caption did not specify the reason for Duterte’s alleged hospitalization. The phrase “See more” is also manually typed into the caption rather than generated by Facebook, and the collage is embedded in a link instead of an album.
Many commenters appear to have accepted the images as authentic, posting prayers and messages wishing Duterte a swift recovery.

The facts: The photos were generated using artificial intelligence. AI detection tools Hive Detect and Sightengine assessed the images as 99.5% and 87% likely to be AI-generated or deepfake content, respectively.

Duterte has been held at the ICC detention facility in The Hague, The Netherlands since his March 2025 arrest. Neither the ICC nor any credible news outlet has reported that he was transported to a hospital.
Duterte at the ICC: The misleading posts emerged shortly before Duterte’s trial, which is scheduled to begin on November 30.

Trial Chamber III will determine whether the former leader is guilty beyond reasonable doubt of murder and attempted murder as crimes against humanity, related to his anti-illegal drug campaign in Davao as mayor and vice mayor, allegedly carried out through the Davao Death Squad, and subsequently nationwide after he became president in 2016.

Prosecutors plan to present around 100 witnesses, with five expected to testify before the court recesses for the holidays on December 18. (READ: Here’s what to expect at the opening of Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC trial)

Supreme Court update: On November 24, the Supreme Court dismissed petitions questioning Duterte’s arrest. The High Court ruled that the petitions were moot because a writ of habeas corpus cannot be enforced beyond Philippine jurisdiction and Duterte is already in ICC custody. Nine justices voted to dismiss the petitions, while four dissented.

The Court clarified that the dismissal does not imply that Duterte’s arrest and transfer to The Hague were necessarily legal, and that any claims of rights violations must be pursued through other legal proceedings.
Debunked: Rappler has fact-checked claims regarding Duterte’s health condition:

items: FACT CHECK: No proof of Duterte in ‘critical’ condition
FACT CHECK: Photo of bedridden Duterte is fake, digitally altered

blocks.text: – Agatha Gonzalvo/Rappler.com
Agatha Gonzalvo is a Research and Data volunteer at Rappler. She is a fourth-year Applied Economics student at De La Salle University Manila.

articles.title: Marcos breaks ground on P2.2-B water supply project in Iloilo City
articles.summary: President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. broke ground Friday on the P2.2-billion Jalaur Bulk Water Supply Project in Sta. Barbara, Iloilo, which is expected to deliver up to 86 million liters per…

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 1:42pm

President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. broke ground Friday on the P2.2-billion Jalaur Bulk Water Supply Project in Sta. Barbara, Iloilo, which is expected to deliver up to 86 million liters per day upon completion.
Speaking at the groundbreaking activity at the Metro Iloilo Bulk Water Facility in Barangay Talanghauan, Marcos said the project will increase water supply in the area by 2029.

"Water is essential to our health, to our livelihoods, the growth of our communities, and the food that we produce, to the businesses that we operate, so much of our daily, our very lives for that matter depend on having a sufficient and reliable water supply," Marcos said.

"Once completed, the project will provide an additional capacity of 86 million liters per day for Iloilo City and its seven districts, bringing the combined capacity to 136 million liters per day. With this additional supply, the Metro Iloilo Water District (MWID) aims to double its water service connections from 52,000 presently to 150,000 by 2029," the President added.

The P2.2-billion project, Marcos said, will complement the dams of Jalaur Multi-purpose Project Stage 2, which he inaugurated in July 2024. These systems are expected to improve water pressure and provide round-the-clock access to safe drinking water.
El Niño's impact

Marcos said MWID's coverage is just at 30% of households in Iloilo city, as drought associated with El Niño has exacerbated water shortages and placed further pressure on our existing water resources.

"As we now address the immediate challenges that are presented to us by El Niño, we must also look beyond that. As of the 5th of November, three major river irrigation systems in Iloilo have already reported significant declines in water levels. And that's why I've directed our concerned government agencies to use irrigation dams to supplement bulk water supply projects and to strengthen water security, especially in underserved areas," Marcos said.

Metro Pacific Water Chairman Manny Pangilinan, who also present during the groundbreaking, said the project will make the Metro Pacific-funded desalination plant in Iloilo city as a plug-and-play combo of power and water.

"For families, that means safer water at home. For businesses, it means room to grow. Any city that wants new offices and factories must be able to promise more reliable water first," Pangilinan said.

"On the surface, this appears to be a story only about pipes and permits. But when government and private sector have the will to engage in complex conversations about who does what—and actually choose to execute—things get done. This is what we need more of in our country," Pangilinan added.
Marcos agreed with Pangilinan, saying that water from the Jalaur River will travel through the high-line canal to a designated tapping point.

"From the tapping point here, it will be conveyed to a treatment facility. It will then be made safe for consumption before being distributed to our communities, to our households," Marcos said. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Venezuela to scrap law that bars opposition from public office
articles.summary: The legislation has been criticised for enabling political persecution since it was introduced two years ago.

blocks.text: Venezuela will repeal a law that bars opposition figures from assuming public office, the speaker of the National Assembly Jorge Rodríguez has said.
The legislation, which was introduced two years ago, has been criticised for enabling political persecution, but Rodríguez said no politician had been subjected to its provisions.
The older brother of Venezuela's interim president Delcy Rodríguez said he expected the reforms to be approved next week.
Delcy Rodríguez's interim government has been negotiating with opposition parties since taking over at the start of the year, when former President Nicolás Maduro was seized by the United States.
The legislation, known as the Simón Bolívar Law, was passed shortly after the election in July 2024 in which then-incumbent Maduro was declared the winner amid widespread allegations of fraud.
Under the legislation, individuals who requested or supported foreign sanctions against Venezuela were permanently banned from political office and had their assets confiscated.
"Legislative processes are dynamic processes. That law responded to a very specific moment in a particular situation that Venezuela was going through," Jorge Rodríguez said.

During subsequent talks, which began in August, the interim government and parts of the opposition agreed to review several other laws as part of a "route map towards democracy", according to an opposition statement.
Delcy Rodríguez has promised that the South American country will hold free and fair elections, without setting a date.
Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado is widely expected to run for office in the event of an election despite being excluded from transition talks.
Machado returned to the country in October after more than 10 months in exile.
In the 2024 election, Machado's ally Edmundo González ran in her place after she was barred from running for office by Maduro's government.
The electoral authority, which was closely aligned with the government, declared Maduro the winner without making detailed voting tallies public.
The opposition argued that González won the election, not Maduro, uploading copies of the voting tallies as evidence.

articles.title: Erin Patterson launches high court appeal bid over mushroom murder convictions
articles.summary:
Patterson, 52, seeks leave to appeal to Australia’s highest court over deaths of estranged family members after fatal beef wellington lunch

  • Get our

blocks.text: Erin Patterson has applied to the high court seeking leave to appeal after a failed bid last month to overturn her triple murder conviction.
Patterson, 52, was found guilty last year of the murders of her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt Heather Wilkinson, after she hosted them for lunch.
She was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived eating beef wellington laced with death cap mushrooms after spending weeks in hospital.
On Friday afternoon, her lawyers filed her application to try to overturn her convictions and life sentence in the high court, a source confirmed to Guardian Australia.

Victoria’s court of appeal last month ruled Patterson’s appeal against her convictions should be dismissed. But it granted an appeal by the director of public prosecutions against Patterson’s sentence, finding that her original sentence of life imprisonment with a non-parole period of 33 years was too lenient. She was resentenced to life without parole.

“This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms,” court of appeal justices Lesley Taylor, Stephen McLeish and Peter Kidd found in their judgment on 30 October.

“Necessarily, we have given the question whether it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period anxious consideration, in light of the gravity of such a conclusion and the different view to which the experienced sentencing judge came.
“But the features of the offending … lead each of us to conclude that this is a case of such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period.”
Patterson had 28 days from that judgment to apply for special leave to appeal to the high court, a period that ended on Friday.
Her written application for leave to appeal is expected to be determined by all seven high court justices.
If they cannot make a determination based on the written application, the justices can refer the application to a hearing for oral argument.
Applications are typically referred to the justices the week before a sitting period and considered that Monday, before decisions are published the following Thursday.
after newsletter promotion
The high court’s last sitting period of the year runs from 30 November to 11 December, meaning Patterson could know the fate of her application within the next fortnight.
If not, the court does not sit again until 1 February. The court would not comment on the application.
Patterson’s lawyers had previously argued in the court of appeal that her convictions should be overturned on seven grounds, all but two of which were dismissed without leave to appeal granted.

The two grounds for which Patterson was granted leave to appeal, but were also dismissed, related to the sequestration of the jury during their deliberations, and the telephone cell tower and iNaturalist evidence presented during her trial.
The court heard that the jury in the case stayed at the same motel as the police informant and DPP staff while they were deciding on their verdicts in the trial.

Patterson argued that this represented “a fundamental irregularity … that has fatally undermined the integrity of the verdicts and requires the quashing of the convictions and an order for a re-trial so that justice can not only be done but be seen to be done”.

The second ground was that cell tower evidence, which suggested Patterson could have been in Loch and Outtrim after death cap mushroom sightings were reported in the towns on the citizen science website iNaturalist, should not have been adduced in her trial as it was either irrelevant, or its relevance was “outweighed by its unfair prejudice”.

articles.title: Alan Jones defence opens and closes in space of a few hours as indecent assault trial draws to a close
articles.summary:
Former broadcaster, 85, has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of sexual touching and indecent assault

  • Get our

blocks.text: Alan Jones’s defence in his indecent assault and sexual touching trial has lasted only a few hours, with closing submissions in the long-running case due next week.

Jones’s barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC opened the defence case on Friday by stating, “I am not calling the defendant,” ending months of speculation about whether the former broadcaster, 85, would give evidence.
Jones has pleaded not guilty to 19 indecent assault and two sexual touching charges brought by five men who allege the offences took place between 2003 and 2020.
On Friday afternoon, after a break for the crown to read the defence submissions, Bashir presented two medical reports and a restaurant receipt, along with a corresponding bank statement.
After half an hour of objections to the documents by the crown, Bashir said: “Your honour, that closes the defence.”
No witnesses were called on Friday although some defence witnesses were called by the crown during the four-month trial.
The prosecutor Georgina Wright objected to the restaurant documents on the basis they carried no weight “whatsoever” – but judge Glenn Walsh admitted them.
Bashir argued the documents were relevant to the “credibility and reliability” of complainant C, who alleged he was assaulted by Jones at an end of year lunch at a north shore restaurant.

The alleged victim, a former driver for Jones, earlier told the court that Jones had instructed him to sit next to him and then spent the entire lunch with his left hand under the table either on his leg or on his penis over his pants.
The defence has argued the end of year lunch took place at a different north shore restaurant and presented a receipt for that establishment for $1,247.
Jason Morrison, a former 2GB colleague of Jones, earlier told the court he recalled a different name of the restaurant to complainant C and other witnesses.
“This has been a big trial,” Walsh said. “There are something like 290 or so exhibits and about 5,000-odd pages worth of transcripts.”
The judge gave the parties four days to prepare closing submissions, which are scheduled to begin on Thursday.
after newsletter promotion

The judge-only trial has sat for 70 days at Sydney’s Downing Centre local court and the defendant has been present for all the evidence. Jones has sat in the front row next to his solicitor Bryan Wrench.
The youngest complainant, known as complainant A, alleged that Jones touched him on the bottom when he stayed overnight at Jones’s Fitzroy Falls farm when he was 17.

The trial has heard from a prominent athlete, known as complainant M, who told the court Jones would welcome him with a hug and a kiss on the cheek and use flattering terms like “champion” and “beautiful man”.

M told the court the defendant kissed him and pressed his genitalia against his thigh causing him to shout out “OK mate” and flee Jones’s harbourside apartment. He alleged that on another occasion Jones kissed him on the side of his mouth at an awards night.
Jones has denied all wrongdoing and said the allegations were either baseless or distorted the truth.
Bashir has said the alleged victims were egged on to complain by media rivals, and that their reliability and credibility were questionable.
Media rivals, Bashir alleged in her opening statements, included shock jock Ray Hadley and Sydney Morning Herald columnist Peter FitzSimons.

articles.title: Race hate exploded in this Spanish town last year. Now its residents are bracing for more
articles.summary:
Torre-Pacheco’s diverse communities are fearful that the far-right Vox party will enter government after Sunday’s election

Sitting on a park bench, taking in the sunny day, Naima reflected…

blocks.text: Sitting on a park bench, taking in the sunny day, Naima reflected on all that had seemingly changed since she moved to Spain three decades earlier.

Back then, the Moroccan national had felt warmly welcomed by Spaniards. “I had never, at any point in my life, felt like there was racism,” she said. “But now things are changing. And the blame lies with rightwing politics.”

Over the years, she has steadily watched as a growing crop of politicians sought to win votes by demonising migrants, minorities and Muslims. The impact reverberated deeply in places such as Torre-Pacheco, whose fertile fields and constant demand for farmhands has long attracted workers from around the world.

“They peddle racism, and lots of people end up suffering,” said Naima, 53. “Here everyone knows me, but others speak of being treated differently, looked at in a certain way, or having gestures made at them.”
On Sunday, Spain is set to gain a glimpse of how deeply engrained these divisions have become as voters cast their ballots in a snap general election.

Most polls suggest the government of the Socialist leader, Pedro Sánchez, will be replaced by a rightwing coalition led by the conservative People’s party (PP) and supported by the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party. If so, it will be the first time that a far-right party has governed Spain since the return to democracy after the death of General Franco.

blocks.caption: Migrants make up almost a third of the 42,000-strong population of Torre-Pacheco in Murcia. Photograph: José Miguel Fernández/The Guardian

blocks.text: The possibility has left many in Torre-Pacheco, where migrants make up at least 30% of the 42,000 residents, worried about what comes next, according to cafe owner Allal Abourayane. “A lot of people are afraid of Vox,” he said. “They’re worried about what the party will mean for their children’s futures.”

In the lead-up to Sunday’s vote, the far-right party has pointedly targeted people from north African countries, announcing plans that include revising the nationalisation of more than 300,000 people of Moroccan origin and limiting the number of pupils from “other cultures or with insufficient command of Spanish” in classrooms.

Other Vox initiatives have more broadly targeted all migrants, such as a promise to impose a tax on remittances similar to the one launched last year in the US by Donald Trump’s administration. Last year, a party official briefly floated the idea of deporting up to 8 million people of foreign origin, including the children of immigrants, before the party backtracked. In September, another official reportedly told the country’s major corporations of plans to lower the cost of housing by expelling 1.5 million migrants.

The PP has responded by hardening its discourse, with promises to bar the burqa and niqab in public spaces and expand the process of residency renewal to include Spanish language tests and constitutional knowledge questions. This sparked wider questions as to what this could mean for some British or American pensioners and digital nomads living in Spain.

On the tree-lined streets of Torre-Pacheco, many were swift to point to the risks of this discourse. They speak from first-hand experience: the Murcian town made headlines last year when extremists from across Spain arrived, intent on exacting revenge after reports of an assault on an elderly man.

The pensioner had told local media he believed his attacker was of north African origin. This sent racist messaging on social media rocketing by 1,500%, according to tracking by the central government.

In Torre-Pacheco, locals watched in shock as the hatred leapt off social media platforms and on to their streets. As baton-wielding groups roamed the town for two nights, determined to “hunt” down people with foreign origins, the mayor called on migrants to stay indoors. Some refused, leading to clashes between the extremists and small groups of residents, at times carrying Moroccan flags.

At least 10 people were arrested, including three young men of north African background who were linked to the attack on the elderly man. Six Spaniards and a Moroccan national were also detained on accusations including assault, public disorder and hate crimes.

blocks.caption: Antonio León, a former mayor of Torre-Pacheco, says the town has become synonymous with hatred because of anti-migrant violence. Photograph: José Miguel Fernández/The Guardian

blocks.text: More than 16 months later, many are still coming to grips with those events. “The hatred came from the outside,” said Antonio León, a politician with the Independent party and mayor of the city from 2015 to 2023. “We’ve always lived together peacefully. People here didn’t take part in what happened, they understand the social and cultural diversity we have in this town.”

Even so, Torre-Pacheco had now become synonymous with extreme hate, he said. “The name Torre-Pacheco has been tainted. Everywhere I go in Spain, I say I’m from here, and they associate me with what happened.”

The Socialist-led central government was unequivocal in linking the events to the discourse of the far right. Its representative in Murcia, Mariola Guevara, said at the time: “We are normalising and giving space in institutions to radicalised, xenophobic, racist political organisations that constantly incite hatred and associate any kind of crime with immigration.”

As the blame game played out, those who had been targeted were left with lingering scars, said Abourayane. “Something has shifted here,” he said. “There are people who are still fearful or who don’t feel as comfortable here as they used to.”

blocks.caption: Ousama Alalo, a political scientist from Torre-Pacheco, says migrants are an easy target for far-right politicians. Photograph: José Miguel Fernández/The Guardian

blocks.text: It was a hint of how things could play out if Vox ends up securing a role in Spain’s central government, said Ousama Alalo, a political scientist from Torre-Pacheco.

The region of Murcia, whose economy is deeply reliant on migrant labour to sustain its global exports of fruit and vegetables, burst into the spotlight in the 2019 general elections after Vox emerged as the most popular party there. It soon became a prominent force in the region, transforming Murcia into what analysts have described as a “laboratory” for anti-migrant policies.
“The People’s party doesn’t have the necessary majorities to govern, so they look to Vox,” said Alalo. “So then what happens? Migrants become an easy bargaining chip.”

The result was a series of measures that have targeted Muslims and migrants in Murcia, from a ban on religious gatherings in sports centres that mainly affected Muslims in Jumilla to the scrapping of an extracurricular scheme that had allowed 350 children to learn Arabic and about Moroccan culture.

“They’ve been trying and testing things again and again – everything works here in Murcia,” said Alalo, who is among a group that has sought to counter these initiatives with the launch of the Platform for the Rights of the Muslim Community in Murcia. “To them we’re an easy target, we’re vulnerable and don’t have political power.”

The discrimination coming from the top levels of the regional government has added to the challenges for a population that was already deeply marginalised, Alalo added. “Right now we’re in the neighbourhood of San Antonio, where about 60% of the population hails from abroad and the average income is €10,600,” he said – less than half the average salary in the region.
“Many of them live in deteriorating houses, there’s a lot of school absenteeism and young people who can’t see a future for themselves, all while they’re being discriminated against.”

blocks.caption: Nabil Moreno, the president of the Al Manar Islamic Community in Torre-Pacheco, says the economic contribution of migrants is ignored. Photograph: José Miguel Fernández/The Guardian

blocks.text: The result had left some migrants feeling as though they are waging battle on multiple fronts, according to Nabil Moreno, the president of the Al Manar Islamic Community in Torre-Pacheco.

Many were grappling with issues common across Spain, such as the soaring cost of housing, but with the added burden of being demonised by rightwing forces who seize on every conflict and every issue involving them, he said. “We’ve been in this city for 30 to 40 years, we have families, we contribute to the economy. Many of us have helped to grow the economy of this town. But of course, nobody talks about this.”

The view was echoed by Naima, who said the far right would probably do little to curb migration once in power. “We work in their homes, we work in their fields, we work in everything, they’re never going to throw us out,” she said.

Instead, she felt racism was being used to rally people behind a platform that would ultimately prove disastrous to many in Spain. “If the rightwing forces win the election, the middle class will be screwed. Retirees, schoolchildren – people will see their rights rolled back,” she said. “They’re not only going after foreigners. Hopefully people won’t be taken in by all of this.”
